title: Basic system and network administration
content:
## Overview

FortiGate is a robust, multifunctional security device that can act in different modes or roles to address different network requirements. In today's complex environments, networks run vertically from the LAN to the internet, and horizontally from the physical network to the private virtual network and to the cloud. FortiGate can be deployed as a data-center firewall, as an ISFW to contain a network breach, and can also function as DNS and DHCP servers configured to provide web filter, antivirus, and IPS services.

![Basic system and network administration](diagram:0)

## Operating Modes

When you deploy FortiGate, you can choose between two operating modes:

- **NAT mode** (default): FortiGate routes packets based on layer 3, like a router. Each logical network interface has an IP address, and FortiGate determines the egress interface based on the destination IP address and entries in its routing tables.
- **Transparent mode**: FortiGate forwards packets at layer 2, like a switch. Its interfaces have no IP addresses, and FortiGate identifies the egress interface based on the destination MAC address. The device in transparent mode has an IP address used for management traffic.

NAT mode is the default operation mode. In each firewall policy, you can enable or disable UTM and NGFW modules.

## Initial Setup

To access the GUI on FortiGate or FortiWiFi, open a web browser and visit `https://192.168.1.99`. The default login information is public knowledge — never leave the default password blank.

All FortiGate models have a console port, or USB management port, or both. You can access the CLI using the CLI console widget on the GUI or from a terminal emulator such as PuTTY or Tera Term.

You can configure the **interface role** (WAN, LAN, Undefined). Settings that do not apply to the current role are hidden on the GUI, preventing accidental misconfiguration. For example, when the role is configured as WAN, there is no DHCP server and device detection configuration available. You can give interfaces **aliases** (for example, calling port3 `internal_network`) to make your list of policies easier to comprehend.

Interface IP addresses can be assigned:
- Manually (static)
- Automatically using DHCP
- Automatically using PPPoE (available on the CLI)

The built-in DHCP server supports advanced options including DNS servers, NTP configurations, DHCP relay to forward requests to an external server, and custom IP address assignment rules to map specific IP addresses to MAC addresses.

## Routing Configuration

Before integrating FortiGate into your network, you should configure a default gateway. You must configure a **static route** with destination `0.0.0.0/0` to forward traffic through the network interface connected to the internet. Without this, FortiGate will not be able to respond to packets outside the subnets directly attached to its own interfaces and may fail to connect to FortiGuard.

FortiGate hardware uses application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) such as a content processor (CP) or network processor (NP) chip for cryptography and packet forwarding, delivering dramatically better performance compared to single-purpose devices.

> **Key terms:** RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is not a valid IP assignment method.

> **Key terms:** Setting the role to Undefined displays all options, including those normally hidden by other roles.

title: Basic administration
content:
## Overview

FortiGate supports multiple management interfaces. Most features are available on both the GUI and CLI, but there are a few exceptions. You cannot view reports on the CLI. Advanced settings and diagnostic commands for super users are usually not available on the GUI. As you become more familiar with FortiGate, you might want to use the CLI, API, or FortiManager in addition to the GUI.

You can access the CLI through the JavaScript widget on the GUI named **CLI Console**, or through a terminal emulator such as Tera Term or PuTTY. Your terminal emulator can connect through the network via SSH, or the local console port. SNMP and some other administrative protocols are also supported, but they are read-only.

![Basic administration](diagram:0)

## Administrator Profiles

When assigning permissions to an administrator profile, you can specify **read-and-write**, **read-only**, or **none** to each area.

By default, there is a special profile named `super_admin`, which is used by the account named `admin`. You cannot change it. It provides full access to everything, making the admin account similar to a root superuser account.

You can create custom profiles. For example, a profile named `auditor_access` with read-only permissions. Restricting a person's permissions to those necessary for his or her job is a best practice — even if that account is compromised, the compromise to your FortiGate device is not total.

The **Override Idle Timeout** option allows the `admintimeout` value, under `config system accprofile`, to be overridden for each access profile. This lets you configure administrator profiles to increase inactivity timeout and facilitate use of the GUI for central monitoring on a per-profile basis.

## Trusted Hosts and Secure Access

Another way to secure FortiGate is to define the hosts or subnets that are **trusted sources** from which to log in. If an administrator attempts to log in from a machine with any other IP address, they will receive an authentication failure message.

If you leave any IPv4 address as `0.0.0.0/0`, it means that connections from any source IP address will be allowed. By default, `0.0.0.0/0` is the configuration for the administrator.

Be aware of any NAT that occurs between the specified device and FortiGate. You can easily prevent an administrator from logging in from the specified IP address if it is later NATed to another address before reaching FortiGate.

## Administrative Access and Protocols

You can choose whether to allow concurrent sessions. Allowing concurrent settings lets an administrator open multiple browser tabs and CLI sessions at the same time. Disallow concurrent sessions to avoid accidentally overwriting settings.

For better security, use only secure protocols, and enforce password complexity and changes.

The **Idle timeout** setting specifies the number of minutes before an inactive administrator session times out (the default is 5 minutes). A shorter idle timeout is more secure.

Management protocols are configured per-interface: HTTPS, HTTP, PING, and SSH. Enabling PING on an internal interface is useful for troubleshooting. However, if it is an external interface exposed to the internet, the PING protocol could expose FortiGate to a denial of service (DoS) attack.

Key protocols and their purposes:
- **FortiTelemetry**: managing FortiClient and the Security Fabric
- **CAPWAP**: for FortiAP, FortiSwitch, and FortiExtender managed by FortiGate
- **FMG-Access**: communicating with FortiManager
- **RADIUS accounting**: for single sign-on (SSO) authentication
- **FTM (FortiToken Mobile push)**: second-factor authentication requests

> **Key terms:** Viewing reports is available in the GUI but not the CLI.

title: FortiGuard subscription
content:
## Overview

FortiGuard Subscription Services provide FortiGate with up-to-date threat intelligence. Some FortiGate services connect to other servers, such as FortiGuard, in order to work. FortiGate uses FortiGuard by:

- Periodically requesting packages that contain a new engine and signatures
- Querying the FDN (FortiGuard Distribution Network) on an individual URL or host name

By default, the FortiGuard server location is set to anywhere — FortiGate selects a server based on server load, from any part of the world. You have the option to change the FortiGuard server location to USA, in which case FortiGate selects a USA-based FortiGuard server.

![FortiGuard subscription](diagram:0)

## Query and Package Updates

FortiGuard queries are **real-time**: FortiGate asks the FDN every time it scans for spam or filtered websites. FortiGate uses queries (rather than downloading the database) because of the size and frequency of changes that occur to the database. You can select queries to use **UDP** or **HTTPS** for transport. These protocols are designed for speed, not fault tolerance, so queries require that your FortiGate device has a reliable internet connection.

**Packages**, like antivirus and intrusion prevention system (IPS), are smaller and do not change as frequently — they are downloaded (in many cases) only once a day. They are downloaded using **TCP** for reliable transport. After the database is downloaded, their associated FortiGate features continue to function even if FortiGate does not have reliable internet connectivity.

When using FortiGuard servers for DNS, FortiOS uses **DNS over TLS (DoT)** by default to secure the DNS traffic.

## Checking FortiGuard Status

You can check the status of FortiGuard licenses and the communication to FortiGuard on the FortiGate GUI. You can also check the versions of the locally installed databases for each of the FortiGuard services.

The CLI command to list all FortiGuard databases and engines installed displays information including:
- Version
- Contract expiration date
- Time it was updated
- What happened during the last update

The list includes antivirus, IPS, application, mobile malware definitions, and other security services. FortiGate is licensed and updated using FortiGuard services.

## Secure Processing Units (SPU)

FortiGate uses network processor (NP) and content processor (CP) chips — collectively known as **secure processing units (SPU)** — to offload processing. These are specially designed integrated circuits that improve performance and increase processing speeds on FortiGate. The NP and CP processors handle tasks such as cryptography and packet forwarding more efficiently than a CPU alone.

title: The FortiGate log workflow
content:
## Overview

When traffic passes through FortiGate to your network, FortiGate scans the traffic and then acts based on the firewall policies in place. FortiGate records this activity and stores the information in a log message. The log message is stored in a log file, which is then stored on a device capable of storing logs. FortiGate can store logs locally or send them to an external storage device, such as FortiAnalyzer.

Logs help you monitor your network traffic, locate problems, establish baselines, and more. For effective logging, your FortiGate system date and time should be accurate. Fortinet recommends using an NTP server. FortiGate is used as NTP server by default.

![The FortiGate log workflow](diagram:0)

## Log Types

FortiGate has three types of logs: traffic, event, and security. Each type is divided into subtypes.

- **Traffic logs** record traffic flow information such as HTTP/HTTPS requests. Subtypes include forward, local, and sniffer.
  - Forward traffic logs contain information about traffic that FortiGate either accepted or rejected according to a firewall policy.
  - Local traffic logs contain information about traffic sent directly to and from the FortiGate management IP addresses.
  - Sniffer logs contain information related to traffic seen by the one-arm sniffer.
- **Event logs** record system and administrative events, such as adding or modifying a setting, or daemon activities. Subtypes include system, user, router, VPN, WAD, HA, and wireless.
  - System event logs contain information related to operations, such as automatic FortiGuard updates and GUI logins.
  - User logs contain login and logoff events for firewall policies with user authentication.
- **Security logs** record security events such as virus attacks and intrusion attempts. They contain log entries based on the security profile type (log type = utm), including application control, antivirus, DLP, antispam, web filter, intrusion protection, anomaly (DoS policy), and web application firewall (WAF).

## Log Levels

Each log entry includes a log level (or priority level) that ranges in order of importance from emergency to information. There is also a debug level, which adds diagnostic information to an event log. The debug level is rarely used, unless you are actively investigating an issue with Fortinet Support.

Generally, the lowest log level you should use is information, but even this level generates many logs and can cause premature hard disk failure. Depending on the type of log and your organization's needs, you may want to use only notification logs or higher.

## Log Message Structure

Every log message has a standard layout comprising two sections: a header and a body.

- The **header** contains fields common to all log types: originating date and time, log identifier, log category, severity level, and VDOM.
- The **body** describes the reason the log was created and the actions that FortiGate took. Key body fields include:
  - `policyid` — which firewall rule matched the traffic
  - `srcip` — the source IP address
  - `dstip` — the destination IP address
  - `hostname` — the URL or IP of the host
  - `action` — what FortiGate did when it found a matching policy
  - `msg` — the reason for the action taken

For information about log structures and associated meanings, visit http://docs.fortinet.com.

> **Key terms:** Security logs created within the security profile cause the menu item to appear; if no security logs exist, the menu item does not appear.

title: The log storage options
content:
## Local Disk Logging

Typically, mid-level to high-end FortiGate models have a hard drive. FortiGate can store logs on its hard drive, which is known as local logging or disk logging. Depending on the model series, disk logging may be enabled by default.

FortiGate can store all log types, including log archives and traffic logs, locally. Under heavy log usage, disk logging will result in a performance impact. If you want to store logs locally on FortiGate, you must enable disk logging on the Log Settings page. Only some FortiGate models support disk logging.

You must enable disk logging in order for information to appear on the FortiView dashboards. If disabled, logs display in real time only. You can also enable this setting using the CLI `config log disk setting` command. By default, logs older than seven days are deleted from the disk. This value is configurable.

![The log storage options](diagram:0)

## External Storage Options

You can configure FortiGate to store logs on syslog servers, FortiCloud, FortiSIEM, FortiAnalyzer, or FortiManager. Whenever possible, it is preferred to store logs externally.

- **Syslog**: A logging server used as a central repository for networked devices.
- **FortiCloud**: A Fortinet subscription-based, hosted security management and log retention service that offers long-term storage of logs with reporting. Every FortiGate offers a free tier keeping logs for seven days; you must upgrade to the paid service to retain logs for one year.
- **FortiSIEM**: Provides unified event correlation and risk management that can collect, parse, normalize, index, and store security logs.
- **FortiAnalyzer**: An external logging device with the primary purpose of storing and analyzing logs. Log limits are model dependent but are much higher than FortiManager.
- **FortiManager**: Primarily designed to centrally manage multiple FortiGate devices. Log volumes are limited to a fixed amount per day, which is less than the equivalent size of FortiAnalyzer.

Note that local logging is not required for you to configure logging to FortiAnalyzer or FortiManager.

## FortiAnalyzer Log Processing

FortiAnalyzer first stores incoming logs in raw format for archive purposes. These archived raw logs cannot be viewed using FortiView or Log View. Next, FortiAnalyzer inserts the logs into the SQL database. You can view these logs and run reports on them.

The logging and reporting workflow operates as follows:
1. Registered devices send logs to FortiAnalyzer.
2. FortiAnalyzer collates and stores those logs in a way that makes it easy to search and run reports.
3. Administrators can connect to FortiAnalyzer using the GUI to view the logs manually or generate reports to analyze the data.

## FortiAnalyzer Operating Modes

FortiAnalyzer has two modes of operation: analyzer and collector.

- **Analyzer mode**: FortiAnalyzer acts as a central log aggregator for one or more log collectors. Analyzer mode is the default operating mode.
- **Collector mode**: FortiAnalyzer collects logs from multiple devices and forwards those logs, in their original binary format, to another device such as a FortiAnalyzer operating in analyzer mode. Depending on the forwarding mode, it can also send them to a syslog server or a common event format (CEF) server. A collector does not allow event management or reporting.

You can change the operating mode in the System Information widget on the dashboard.

title: FortiGate registration with FortiAnalyzer
content:
## Registering a Device on FortiAnalyzer

For FortiAnalyzer to start collecting logs from a device, that device must become a registered device on FortiAnalyzer. To FortiAnalyzer, there are only two types of devices: those that are registered and those that are unregistered. A registered device has been authorized to store logs on FortiAnalyzer, whereas an unregistered device is requesting to store logs on FortiAnalyzer.

There are various ways you can register a device with FortiAnalyzer. A supported device can send a registration request, which the FortiAnalyzer administrator can accept or deny. You can also add devices to FortiAnalyzer using the Add Device wizard. You can add a device based on its serial number or a pre-shared key. If the device is supported and all its details are correct, FortiAnalyzer registers the device.

![FortiGate registration with FortiAnalyzer](diagram:0)

## Initiating Registration from FortiGate

There are two ways to initiate a request from a FortiGate device.

In the first method, you must configure the FortiAnalyzer IP address and enable logging on FortiGate. After you click Apply, and if the request reaches FortiAnalyzer successfully, you must confirm the serial number of the FortiAnalyzer device if the Verify FortiAnalyzer certificate setting is enabled.

After the supported device makes the request, it automatically appears under the root ADOM in Device Manager. The FortiAnalyzer administrator should review the details of the unauthorized device and, if satisfied, authorize the device. Upon acceptance of the registration request, you can also assign a device name.

After registering a Fortinet device, you can access it on the Device Manager tab and review details regarding log status and storage utilization.

## Log Upload Options

FortiGate allows near real-time uploading and consistent high-speed compression and analysis to FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager.

If your FortiGate model includes an internal hard drive, the store-and-upload option is available. This allows you to store logs on the disk and then upload them to FortiAnalyzer or FortiManager at a scheduled time, usually a low-bandwidth time. You can configure the store-and-upload option and a schedule on the CLI only.

## Log Transport and Reliable Logging

FortiGate uses UDP port 514 for log transmission by default. When you enable reliable logging on FortiGate, the log transport delivery method changes from UDP to TCP. TCP provides reliable data transfer, guaranteeing that the transferred data remains intact and arrives in the same order in which it was sent.

- If you enable logging to FortiAnalyzer using the FortiAnalyzer GUI, reliable logging is automatically enabled.
- If you enable logging using the CLI, you must explicitly enable reliable logging.
- If you use the FortiGate Fabric Connector to enable FortiAnalyzer logging, reliable logging is not autoenabled.

Logging to FortiCloud uses TCP, and you can set the encryption algorithm using the CLI. The default encryption setting is high. Optionally, if using reliable logging, you can encrypt communications using SSL-encrypted OFTP traffic by configuring the `enc-algorithm` setting on the CLI.

When both FortiGate and FortiAnalyzer are running version 7.2 or later, and reliable logging is configured, FortiGate keeps logs in a confirm queue until it verifies that FortiAnalyzer received them. This is achieved by using sequence numbers (`seq_no`) to track the logs received.

## Log Management Best Practices

Not everything in the network needs to be logged. In your analysis, prioritize factors such as the traffic type, the traffic sources and destinations, and any security events associated with the traffic.

You can enforce global settings to help manage your logs on FortiAnalyzer:
- Specify a global log roll policy to roll or upload logs when the size exceeds a set threshold.
- Specify a global automatic deletion policy for all log files, quarantined files, reports, and content archive files on FortiAnalyzer.

All deletion policies are always active on FortiAnalyzer, so you should carefully configure each policy.

title: The log view
content:
## Viewing Logs on FortiGate GUI

You can access your logs on the GUI in the Log & Report menu. Select the type of log you want to view, such as Security Events. Logs on the GUI appear in a formatted table view. The formatted view is easier to read than the raw view, and it enables you to filter information when viewing log messages. To view the log details, select the log in the table. The log details then appear in the Log Details section on the right side of the window.

If archiving is enabled on security profiles that support it (such as DLP), archived information appears in the Log Details section in the Archived Data section. Archived logs are also recorded when using FortiAnalyzer or FortiCloud.

If you configure FortiGate to log to multiple locations, you can change the log display location in this section. To navigate the logs more efficiently, you can set up log filters. The more information you specify in the filter, the easier it is to find the precise log entry. Filters are configurable for each column of log data on the display.

![The log view](diagram:0)

## Log Filtering and Column Management

FortiGate provides several ways to filter and navigate log data efficiently:

- Click the plus icon to select a filter from the drop-down list.
- If you see data you want to filter on in a log already in the table, you can right-click that data to select the quick filter option. For example, right-click a category name in a webfilter log to filter on all logs with that category name.
- By default, the most common columns are shown, and the less common columns are hidden. To add columns, right-click any column field and select the column in the pop-up menu.
- You can also access log messages generated by individual policies. Right-click the policy for which you want to view all associated logs and select Show Matching Logs. FortiGate takes you to the Forward Traffic page where a filter is automatically set based on the policy universally unique identifier (UUID).

## Viewing Logs on the CLI

You are not restricted to the GUI for viewing log messages. You can also view log messages on the CLI, using the `execute log display` command. This command allows you to see specific log messages that you already configured within the `execute log filter` command.

The `execute log filter` command configures which log messages you will see, how many log messages you can view at one time (a maximum of 1000 lines of log messages), and the type of log messages you can view. Logs appear in the raw format view, which displays them as they appear within the log file.

Like the GUI, if you have configured either a syslog or security information and event management (SIEM) server, you will not be able to view log messages on the CLI.

## Log View on FortiAnalyzer

The log view on FortiAnalyzer allows you to view all log types, in normalized logs format, being received by FortiAnalyzer. You can choose to view logs from specific devices, Fabric groups, or log groups. A log group is a group of devices placed together in a single logical object. Log groups are virtual, so they don't have SQL databases or occupy additional disk space.

Traffic logs allow you to view the traffic traversing the firewalls, including details such as source, destination, service, and action. Security logs allow you to view logs related to unified threat management (UTM) inspection. Event logs are generally related to firewall system operations.

## Summary Dashboards and Historical Logs

You can monitor all enabled security and event log types from their respective summary dashboards. Summary dashboards use multiple widgets to display the top logs for each subtype. The time filter set at the dashboard level affects the information included on all widgets simultaneously.

You can view historical logs with the option to specify a time period. By default, historical logs are displayed. You must be using the historical log view to use the custom view or chart builder features. You can switch from viewing historical logs to viewing logs in real time. When viewing logs in real time, you can pause the view to get a more detailed view of the logs.

title: Identifying the different components of firewall policies
content:
## Overview

A firewall policy is a set of rules that specifies which traffic is allowed through FortiGate and what FortiGate should do when traffic matches a policy. Any traffic passing through a FortiGate must be associated with a firewall policy. The policy determines where traffic goes, how it is handled, and whether it is allowed to pass through.

![Identifying the different components of firewall policies](diagram:0)

## Policy Types and Match Criteria

Common policy types include:
- **Firewall policy**: controls traffic flow through FortiGate
- **Virtual wire pair policy**: controls traffic between interfaces in a virtual wire pair
- **Multicast Policy**: allows multicast packets to pass from one interface to another
- **Local-In Policy**: controls traffic to a FortiGate interface and can restrict administrative access
- **DoS Policy**: checks for anomalous patterns in network traffic that arrives at a FortiGate interface

By default, only Firewall Policy is visible under **Policy and Objects**. Other policy types are available through **Feature Visibility**.

Each policy matches traffic using the following objects:
- **Incoming Interface** and **Outgoing Interface**
- **Source**: IP address, user, internet services (ISDB)
- **Destination**: IP address or internet services
- **Schedule**: specific times to apply the policy
- **Service**: IP protocol and port number

When a packet arrives, FortiGate searches from the top of the policy list. The first matching policy is applied. If no match is found, the traffic is dropped by the **default implicit deny** firewall policy.

## Actions, Inspection Modes, and Order of Precedence

If the **Action** is set to **DENY**, FortiGate drops the session. If the **Action** is set to **ACCEPT**, FortiGate allows the session and applies configured settings such as user authentication, SNAT, antivirus scanning, and web filtering.

FortiGate supports two inspection modes for security profiles:
- **Flow-based inspection**: identifies and blocks threats in real time, requires lower processing resources, recommended for policies that prioritize traffic throughput
- **Proxy-based inspection**: buffers traffic and examines it as a whole before determining an action; supports advanced features like usage quota and web-profile override

Because FortiGate is a **stateful firewall**, you must create only one firewall policy that matches the direction of the traffic that initiates the session. FortiGate automatically remembers the source-destination pair and allows replies.

Policy IDs are permanent identifiers. FortiGate automatically assigns a policy ID when you create a new firewall policy using the GUI. The policy ID never changes, even if you move the rule higher or lower in the sequence. You can enable **Multiple Interface Policies** on the Feature Visibility page to allow multiple interfaces per policy.

## Logging and Best Practices

Policies can be displayed in **Interface Pair View**, **Sequence Grouping View**, or **By Sequence**. Specific policies should be placed at the top, followed by more general policies, because FortiGate evaluates policies from the top of the list.

To move policies efficiently, use **Move by ID** (available in By Sequence or Sequence Grouping View). You can configure **Jump to policy after move** to automatically navigate to the new location.

Logging options include:
- **Log allowed traffic** (default: Security events) — generates logs for applied security profiles
- **All sessions** — generates logs for all sessions
- CLI command `ses-denied-traffic` creates a denied session in the session table to reduce CPU usage
- CLI command `set logtraffic-start enable` generates a log when a session starts
- `block-session-timer` (default 30 seconds) sets how long a denied session is kept in the session table

View traffic logs at **Log & Report > Forward Traffic**. You can also right-click a firewall policy and select **Show matching logs**. Use the policy UUID in the filter field to find matching log records.

To confirm whether your FortiGate supports proxy inspection, run `diagnose hardware sysinfo conserve` on the CLI. If total RAM is less than 2 GB, proxy-based settings are not shown on the GUI.

> **Key terms:** FortiGate evaluates firewall policies from top to bottom in the policy list.

> **Key terms:** UUID allows logs to record policy identifiers, improving integration with FortiManager or FortiAnalyzer.

title: NAT firewall policies
content:
## Overview

Network Address Translation (NAT) is a method that enables a NAT device such as a firewall or router to translate (or map) the IP address in a packet to another IP address, usually for connectivity purposes. If the port information in the packet is also translated, then the translation method is called PAT. NAT provides the following benefits:
- **Security**: the real address of a device is hidden from external networks
- **Public address depletion prevention**: hundreds of computers can share the same public IPv4 address
- **Private address flexibility**: addresses can stay the same even if ISPs change; private addresses can be reused in multiple networks

There are two types of NAT: **SNAT** and **DNAT**. In SNAT, a NAT device translates the source IP address and source port in a packet. In DNAT, a NAT device translates the destination IP address and destination port.

![NAT firewall policies](diagram:0)

## SNAT: Outgoing Interface and IP Pools

To configure SNAT in a firewall policy, enable NAT in the firewall and network options section. There are two options:
1. **Use Outgoing Interface Address**: FortiGate uses the egress interface address as the NAT IP. If there are multiple devices behind FortiGate, FortiGate performs many-to-one NAT (also known as PAT). CLI equivalent: `set nat enable`
2. **Use a dynamic IP pool**: dynamic SNAT that allows FortiGate to map private IP addresses to the first available public address from a pool

IP pools allow sessions leaving the FortiGate firewall to use NAT. An IP pool defines a single IP address or a range of IP addresses to be used as the source address for the duration of the session. There are four types of IP pools:
- **Overload** (default): a many-to-one or many-to-few relationship with port translation
- **One-to-one**: assigns an IP pool address to an internal host on a first-come, first-served basis; if no addresses remain, FortiGate drops packets from unserved hosts
- **Fixed port range**: more common in carrier-grade NAT (CGN) deployments
- **Port block allocation**: also more common in carrier-grade NAT (CGN) deployments

IP pools are usually configured in the same range as the interface IP address.

## DNAT: Virtual IPs (VIPs)

VIPs are DNAT objects. For sessions matching a VIP, the destination address is translated — usually a public internet address is translated to the private network address of a server. VIPs are selected in the firewall policy **Destination** field.

The default VIP type is **Static NAT** — a one-to-one mapping. FortiGate performs DNAT on ingress traffic destined to the external IP address defined in the VIP. You can also select **FQDN** as the VIP type, which allows FortiGate to automatically update the external and internal IP addresses used by the VIP when the FQDN resolved address changes.

Enabling **Port Forwarding** on the VIP instructs FortiGate to redirect the traffic matching the external address and port to the mapped internal address and port. With port forwarding enabled, you can reuse the same external address and map it to different internal addresses and ports, provided the external port is unique.

When you configure a VIP or an IP pool, **ARP reply** is enabled by default. When ARP reply is enabled, FortiGate replies to incoming ARP requests for the external address configured in the VIP and IP pools. It is a best practice to keep ARP reply enabled.

Starting in FortiOS version 7.2.4, the parameter `match-vip` is enabled by default, which allows firewall address objects to match VIPs. Disabling `match-vip` on a DENY policy instructs FortiGate not to check for VIPs during policy evaluation.

## NAT Best Practices

- Avoid misconfiguring an IP pool range: double-check the start and end IP addresses of each IP pool
- Ensure the IP pool address range does not overlap with addresses assigned to FortiGate interfaces or to any hosts on directly connected networks
- If internal and external users access the same servers, configure DNS services so internal users resolve to use the destination internal address instead of its external address defined in the VIP
- Do not configure a NAT rule for inbound traffic unless it is required by an application
- Schedule a maintenance window when making changes to NAT settings configuration, since making changes could create a network outage

title: Routing on FortiGate
content:
## Overview

When FortiGate operates in NAT mode — the default operation mode — FortiGate behaves as an IP router. An IP router is a device that forwards packets between IP networks by performing IP routing: the process of determining the next hop to forward a packet based on the packet destination IP address. FortiGate supports both IPv4 and IPv6 routing.

FortiGate performs routing for two types of traffic:
- **Firewall traffic** (also known as user traffic): traffic that travels through FortiGate
- **Local-out traffic**: traffic generated by FortiGate, usually for management purposes (for example, pinging a device or connecting to FortiGuard to download the latest definitions)

Routing takes place before most security features such as firewall policy evaluation, content inspection, traffic shaping, and SNAT.

![Routing on FortiGate](diagram:0)

## Routing Table: RIB, FIB, and Route Types

FortiGate maintains its routing information in two tables:
- **RIB (Routing Information Base)**: the standard routing table containing active connected, static, and dynamic routes
- **FIB (Forwarding Information Base)**: the routing table from the kernel point of view; contains mostly RIB entries plus system-specific entries. FortiGate performs the actual route lookup against the FIB.

The CLI command `get router info routing-table all` displays the same route entries as the routing monitor widget on the FortiGate GUI.

The routing table contains the following types of routes:
- **Static**: manual routes configured by the administrator
- **Connected**: automatic routes added by FortiOS after an interface is assigned an IP address
- **Dynamic**: routes learned using a dynamic routing protocol such as BGP or OSPF

Routes not shown in the routing table include:
- **Inactive routes**: static and connected routes with interfaces that are administratively down or with links that are down
- **Standby routes**: active routes removed from the routing table because they are duplicates with higher distances
- **Policy routes**: regular policy routes, ISDB routes, and SD-WAN rules — viewed in a separate policy route table

## Route Selection: Distance, Metric, and Priority

FortiGate uses three attributes to select the best route among duplicate routes:

**Distance (Administrative distance)**: the first tiebreaker. The lowest-distance route is considered the best route and installed in the routing table. Other lower-distance routes are standby routes stored in the routing table database only.

**Metric**: used by dynamic routing protocols as a tiebreaker among same-protocol routes. The lower the metric, the higher the preference. RIP uses hop count; OSPF uses cost based on link bandwidth.

**Priority**: breaks ties among static routes with the same distance. The lower the priority value, the higher the preference. The priority attribute is set to 1 by default and applies to all routes except connected routes. For static routes, priority settings are in the **Advanced Options** section.

The route lookup process in FortiOS follows this order:
1. Check **policy routes** (if a match with Forward Traffic action, validate against FIB)
2. Check **ISDB routes**, then **SD-WAN rules**
3. Check the **FIB** for standard routing
4. If no match, drop the packet and send ICMP destination network unreachable

## RPF Check and Practical Tools

For each session, FortiGate performs two route lookups: for the first packet sent by the originator, and for the first reply packet from the responder. After completing these lookups, FortiGate writes the routing information to its session table. Subsequent packets are routed according to the session table.

The **RPF (Reverse Path Forwarding) check** protects FortiGate from IP spoofing attacks by verifying a return path to the source in the routing table. Two RPF check modes:
- **Feasible path** (default, formerly called loose): FortiGate verifies the routing table contains a route matching the source address and the incoming interface
- **Strict**: FortiGate also verifies the matching route is the best route in the routing table

You can use firewall address objects (type Subnet or FQDN) as the destination of static routes by enabling **Routing configuration** in the firewall address configuration. ISDB entries can also be applied to static routes to selectively route traffic through specific WAN interfaces; ISDB routes take precedence as policy routes.

The **Route Lookup** tool on the routing monitor widget allows you to look up a destination address (and optionally port, source address, protocol, and source interface) to identify the matching route.

> **Key terms:** RIP uses hop count, which is the number of routers a packet must pass through.

title: ECMP routing
content:
## Overview

Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) routing occurs when two or more routes of the same type have the same destination, distance, metric, and priority. FortiGate installs all of these ECMP routes in the routing table and load balances traffic among them.

ECMP enables you to use multiple paths for the same destination as well as provide built-in failover. You can use ECMP for mission-critical services that require high availability, and also for bandwidth aggregation — leveraging the bandwidth of multiple links by load balancing sessions across them.

![ECMP routing](diagram:0)

## ECMP Load Balancing Algorithms

ECMP can load balance sessions using one of the following four algorithms:

- **Source IP** (default algorithm): FortiGate uses the same ECMP route to route sessions sourced from the same address
- **Source-destination IP**: FortiGate uses the same ECMP route to route sessions with the same source-destination IP address pair
- **Weighted**: applies to static routes only; FortiGate load balances sessions based on the route weight or the respective interface weight — the higher the weight, the more sessions FortiGate routes through the selected route
- **Usage (spillover)**: FortiGate sends sessions to the interface of the first ECMP route until the bandwidth of the interface reaches the configured spillover limit; after the spillover limit is reached, FortiGate uses the interface of the next ECMP route

## Configuring ECMP

If SD-WAN is disabled, you can change the ECMP load balancing algorithm on the FortiGate CLI using the `v4-ecmp-mode` setting. When SD-WAN is enabled, FortiOS hides the `v4-ecmp-mode` setting and replaces it with the `load-balance-mode` setting under `config system sdwan`.

For spillover to work, you must configure the egress and ingress spillover thresholds. The thresholds are set to 0 by default, which disables the spillover check. If you disable SD-WAN, FortiGate selects the lowest numbered interface first.

For a weighted algorithm, you must configure the weights at the interface level or route level. If two or more routes are added to the routing table and you set `v4-ecmp-mode` to `weight-based`, FortiGate routes sessions based on the weight value of each route.

## ECMP with SD-WAN

When SD-WAN is enabled, the `load-balance-mode` setting under `config system sdwan` controls the ECMP algorithm. The main difference between `load-balance-mode` and `v4-ecmp-mode` is that `load-balance-mode` supports an additional **volume** algorithm that `v4-ecmp-mode` does not support.

The **volume algorithm** (available when SD-WAN is enabled) instructs FortiGate to track the cumulative number of bytes of each member and to distribute sessions based on the weight. The higher the weight, the higher the target volume of the interface and, as a result, the more traffic FortiGate sends to it.

When SD-WAN is enabled, weight and spillover thresholds are defined on the SD-WAN member configuration. When SD-WAN is disabled, weight and spillover thresholds are defined on the static route and interface settings, respectively.

If the route over one ECMP link is removed from the routing table, FortiGate automatically starts to forward the traffic through the remaining ECMP routes, providing built-in failover. While ECMP enables you to leverage multiple WAN links on FortiGate, you may want to use SD-WAN because of the additional benefits.

title: Remote authentication
content:
## Why Remote Authentication Matters

Traditional firewalling grants network access by verifying the source IP address and device. This is inadequate and can pose a security risk because the firewall cannot determine who is using the device. FortiGate includes authentication of users and user groups, enabling you to follow individuals across multiple devices.

Where access is controlled by a user or user group, users must authenticate by entering valid credentials such as username and password. After FortiGate validates the user, FortiGate applies firewall policies and profiles to allow or deny access to specific network resources.

FortiGate supports multiple methods of firewall authentication: local password authentication, server-based password authentication (also called remote password authentication), and two-factor authentication.

![Remote authentication](diagram:0)

## Local vs. Server-Based Authentication

**Local password authentication**: User account information (username and password) is stored locally on the FortiGate device. This method works well for a single FortiGate installation. Local accounts are created on the User Definition page.

**Server-based password authentication**: A remote authentication server authenticates users. This method is desirable when multiple FortiGate devices need to authenticate the same users or user groups, or when adding FortiGate to a network that already contains an authentication server. When the server-based method is used, FortiGate does not store all of the user information locally. FortiGate sends the user's entered credentials to the remote authentication server, and the server responds by indicating whether the credentials are valid or not.

There are two options for using external authentication servers:
- **Option 1**: Create user accounts on FortiGate, select the remote authentication server type (RADIUS, TACACS+, or LDAP), and point FortiGate to your preconfigured remote authentication server.
- **Option 2**: Add the remote authentication server to user groups. Create a user group and add the preconfigured remote server to the group. Any user who has an account on the remote authentication server can authenticate.

## LDAP Configuration

Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an application protocol used for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services. The LDAP protocol is used to maintain authentication data that may include departments, people, groups of people, passwords, email addresses, and printers.

Binding is the operation in which the LDAP server authenticates the user. If the user is successfully authenticated, binding allows the user access to the LDAP server, based on that user's permissions. LDAP on port 389 is not secure because it sends the password in clear text. It is highly recommended to use LDAPS, which is more secure. LDAPS uses port 636 for communication.

Key LDAP configuration settings on FortiGate:
- **Distinguished Name (DN)**: Identifies the top of the tree where users are located, generally the dc value.
- **Common Name Identifier**: The attribute name used to find the user name (e.g., `sAMAccountName` or `cn` for Active Directory).
- **Bind Type**: Use Regular bind if searching across multiple domains and requiring credentials of a user authorized to perform LDAP queries.
- **Secure Connection**: Enable and specify LDAPS or STARTTLS plus the CA certificate to secure the connection.

Use Test Connectivity to test whether the connection to the LDAP server is successful. To test user credentials, use Test User Credentials or the `diagnose test authserver` CLI command.

## RADIUS Configuration

RADIUS is a standard protocol that provides authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) services. When a user is authenticating, the client (FortiGate) sends an ACCESS-REQUEST packet to the RADIUS server. The reply from the server is one of the following:
- **ACCESS-ACCEPT**: The user credentials are correct.
- **ACCESS-REJECT**: The credentials are wrong.
- **ACCESS-CHALLENGE**: The server is requesting a secondary password ID, token, or certificate — typically used with two-factor authentication.

Key RADIUS configuration settings:
- **Primary Server IP/Name**: The IP address or FQDN of the RADIUS server.
- **Primary Server Secret**: The secret that was set up on the RADIUS server to allow remote queries from this client.
- **Authentication Method**: Options include chap, pap, mschap, and mschap2. If you select Default, FortiGate will use pap, mschap2, and chap in that order.
- **Include in every User Group**: Adds the RADIUS server and all users who can authenticate against it to every user group on FortiGate — enable only in specific scenarios.

Use the `diagnose test authserver` command on the CLI to test whether a user's credentials can successfully authenticate before implementing it on any firewall policies.

title: Firewall authentication methods
content:
## Active vs. Passive Authentication

All authentication methods—local password authentication, server-based authentication, and two-factor authentication—use active authentication. Active authentication means that users are prompted to manually enter their login credentials before being granted access.

Not all users authenticate in the same way. Some users can be granted access transparently, because user information is determined without asking the user to enter their login credentials. This is known as passive authentication. Passive authentication occurs with the single sign-on method: FSSO, RSSO, and NTLM.

![Firewall authentication methods](diagram:0)

## Two-Factor Authentication

Traditional user authentication requires your username plus something you know, such as a password. The weakness is that if someone obtains your username, they need only your password to compromise your account. Two-factor authentication requires something you know, such as a password, and something you have, such as a token or certificate. Because this method places less importance on often vulnerable passwords, it makes compromising the account more complex for an attacker.

You can use two-factor authentication on FortiGate with both user and administrator accounts. Note that you cannot use two-factor authentication with explicit proxies.

FortiGate can deliver OTPs (one-time passwords) through tokens such as FortiToken 200 (hardware token) and FortiToken Mobile (software token), as well as through email or SMS. OTPs are more secure than static passwords because the passcode changes at regular intervals and is valid for only a short amount of time. FortiTokens generate a new, six-digit password every 60 seconds by default. An NTP server is highly recommended to ensure the OTPs remain in sync.

FortiToken Mobile Push allows users to accept the authorization request from their FortiToken mobile app, without the need to enter an additional code.

Each FortiGate (and FortiGate VM) provides two free FortiToken Mobile activations. You cannot register the same FortiToken on more than one FortiGate. If you want to use the same FortiToken for authentication on multiple FortiGate devices, you must use a central validation server, such as FortiAuthenticator.

## Firewall Policies and Authentication

A firewall policy consists of access and inspection rules that tell FortiGate how to handle traffic. You can use the source of a firewall policy to control authentication. The source of a firewall policy must include the source address (IP address), but you can also include the user and user group. User and user group objects can consist of local firewall accounts, external server accounts, PKI users, and FSSO users.

Active authentication prompts the user for credentials based on the protocol of the traffic and the firewall policy. The firewall policy must specify the allowed protocols such as HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and Telnet. If the firewall policy that has authentication enabled does not allow at least one of the supported protocols used for obtaining user credentials, the user will not be able to authenticate.

DNS is allowed through the firewall before successful user authentication because it is a base protocol. DNS must still be defined in the policy as allowed in order for it to pass. HTTP service is TCP port 80 and does not include DNS (UDP port 53).

## Authentication Behavior and Timeout

When active authentication is used with a fall-through policy that does not have authentication enabled, all traffic will use the fall-through policy, meaning users are not prompted to authenticate. You can change the `auth-on-demand` option via CLI:
- **Implicitly** (default): Will not trigger authentication if there is a fall-through policy.
- **Always**: Triggers an authentication prompt for policies that have active authentication enabled regardless of a fall-through policy. Traffic is not allowed until authentication is successful.

If you want all users on a specific interface to authenticate before accessing any resources, enable captive portal authentication at the interface level.

Authentication timeout options protect against unauthorized access:
- **Idle**: If there are no packets from the host device within the configured timeframe, the user is logged out.
- **Hard**: An absolute time value. Regardless of the user's behavior, the timer starts as soon as the user authenticates and expires after the configured value.
- **New session**: Authentication expires if no new sessions are created through the firewall from the host device within the configured timeout value.

## Monitoring Authenticated Users

You can monitor users who authenticate through your firewall policies using the Dashboard > Assets & Identities > Firewall Users page. It displays the user, user group, duration, IP address, traffic volume, and authentication method. It does not include administrators, because they are not authenticating through firewall policies. This page also allows you to disconnect a user, or multiple users, at the same time.

> **Key terms:** DNS is a base protocol; hostname resolution is almost always a requirement for any protocol to work.

title: Understanding SSO concepts
content:
## Overview

Single Sign-On (SSO) is a process that allows users to be automatically logged in to every application after being identified, regardless of platform, technology, and domain. Fortinet Single Sign-On (FSSO) is a software agent that enables FortiGate to identify network users for security policies or for VPN access, without asking for their username and password.

When a user logs in to a directory service, the FSSO agent sends FortiGate the username, the IP address, and the list of groups that the user belongs to. FortiGate uses this information to maintain a local database of usernames, IP addresses, and group mappings. Because the domain controller authenticates users, FortiGate does not perform authentication.

![Understanding SSO concepts](diagram:0)

## FSSO Deployment Modes

How you deploy and configure FSSO depends on the server that provides your directory services. FSSO for Windows Active Directory (AD) uses a collector agent. There are two working modes that monitor user sign-on activities in Windows:

- **DC agent mode** (recommended): Requires one DC agent installed on each Windows DC. DC agents monitor and forward user login events to the collector agent. The collector agent consolidates events, then forwards them to FortiGate. The collector agent communicates with FortiGate over TCP port 8000 (default) and listens on UDP port 8002 (default).
- **Polling mode**: Can be collector agent-based or agentless. In collector agent-based polling mode, the collector agent uses the SMB (TCP port 445) protocol to periodically request event logs from the domain controllers.
- **Agentless polling mode**: FortiGate polls the DCs directly, instead of receiving login information indirectly from a collector agent. FortiGate uses the SMB protocol to read the event viewer logs from the DCs using only two event IDs: 4768 and 4769.

## Collector Agent-Based Polling Methods

Collector agent-based polling mode has three methods for collecting login information, from most recommended to least:

- **WMI**: A Windows API that gets system information from a Windows server. The collector agent sends WMI queries for user login events to the DC, which reduces network load.
- **WinSecLog**: Polls all the security event logs from the DC. It doesn't miss any login events that have been recorded by the DC, but there can be some delay in large networks.
- **NetAPI**: Polls temporary sessions created on the DC when a user logs in or logs out. It's faster than WMI and WinSecLog; however, it can miss some login events if a DC is under heavy system load.

## FSSO Requirements and Comparison

Regardless of the collector method chosen, some FSSO requirements for your AD network are the same:

- FSSO requires that you have your own DNS server, since Microsoft Windows login events have the workstation name and username, but not the workstation IP address.
- Collector agents need connectivity with all workstations to verify whether users are still logged in.
- DC agent mode is more complex but also more scalable. In polling mode, the collector needs to query every domain controller every few seconds, which grows with each DC added.
- FSSO is typically used with directory service networks, such as Windows Active Directory or Novell eDirectory. The eDirectory agent can obtain information using either the Novell API or LDAP.
- Terminal server (TS) agents are used exclusively for Citrix and terminal services environments and require the Windows Active Directory collector agent or FortiAuthenticator.

> **Key terms:** Sessions can be quickly created and purged from RAM (memory) before the agent polls, causing the NetAPI method to miss some login events.

> **Key terms:** Agentless polling mode requires greater system resources and does not scale as easily.

> **Key terms:** FortiGate selects the appropriate security policy and allows the connection if the user belongs to a permitted group.

title: Configuring the FSSO agents and settings on FortiGate
content:
## Overview

FortiGate FSSO configuration depends on the deployment mode you choose. If FortiGate is acting as a collector for agentless polling mode, you must select Poll Active Directory Server and configure the IP addresses and AD administrator credentials for each DC. FortiGate uses LDAP to query AD to retrieve user group information.

If you have collector agents, using either the DC agent mode or the collector agent-based polling mode, you must select Fortinet Single-Sign-On Agent and configure the IP address and password for each collector agent.

![Configuring the FSSO agents and settings on FortiGate](diagram:0)

## Collector Agent Access Modes

The FSSO collector agent can access Windows AD in one of two modes:

- **Collector Agent mode**: You create group filters on the collector agent. The collector agent can still use Advanced mode to access nested groups.
- **Local mode**: You create group filters on FortiGate, using the LDAP server. If you set FortiGate to Local mode, you must set the collector agent to Advanced mode, otherwise the collector agent does not recognize the group filter sent by FortiGate.

The main difference between AD access modes is the naming convention used:
- **Standard mode** uses the Windows convention, NetBios: `Domain\groups`
- **Advanced mode** uses the LDAP convention: `CN=User, OU=Name, DC=Domain`

Advanced mode supports nested or inherited groups; that is, users can be members of subgroups that belong to monitored parent groups. Additionally, in Advanced mode, FortiGate firewall policy authentication can be applied to individual users, user groups, and OUs. In Standard mode, firewall policy authentication applies to user groups but not to individual users or OUs.

## Installation and Configuration

The FSSO agents are available on the Fortinet Support website. The following are available:
- The DC agent
- The collector agent for Microsoft servers: `FSSO_Setup`
- The collector agent for Novell directories: `FSSO_Setup_edirectory`
- The terminal server agent (TSagent) installer for Citrix and terminal servers: `TSAgent_Setup`

When installing the collector agent, it is always a best practice to install in Advanced mode for new FSSO setups. The default installation folder is named FSAE (Fortinet Server Authentication Extension). You do not need to match the FSSO version with your exact FortiGate firmware version, but you do need to match the DC agent version to the collector agent version.

## Key FSSO Settings and Timers

On the FSSO agent configuration GUI, you can configure settings such as:
- Listening port for communication with DC agents (UDP)
- Listening port for communication with FortiGate (TCP)
- NTLM authentication support, SSL, and password authentication
- Timers for workstation verification, dead entry timeout, and IP address change verification

The FSSO collector agent timers play an important role:
- **Workstation verify interval**: Controls when the collector agent connects to individual workstations on port 139 (or port 445) to verify if a user is still logged in.
- **Dead entry timeout interval**: Applies only to entries with an unverified status; used to age out stale entries.
- **IP address change verify interval**: Checks the IP addresses of logged-in users and updates FortiGate when a user's IP address changes. This is especially important in DHCP or dynamic environments.
- **Cache user group lookup result**: Caches the user group membership for a defined period of time.

The FSSO collector agent allows you to configure a FortiGate group filter to actively control what user login information is sent to each FortiGate device. Low-end FortiGate models support 256 Windows AD user groups; mid-range and high-end models support more. It is also a good practice to add all network service accounts to the Ignore User List, as service accounts tend to overwrite user login events and create issues with identity-based policy matching.

> **Key terms:** FSSO supports Security groups, universal groups, groups inside OUs, and universal groups containing universal groups from child domains.

> **Key terms:** If you change the AD access mode, you must recreate the filters because they vary depending on the mode.

title: FSSO monitoring and troubleshooting
content:
## Overview

Effective FSSO monitoring and troubleshooting requires knowledge of the required ports, log configuration, and diagnostic CLI commands. FSSO has a number of required ports that you must allow through all firewalls, or connections will fail. These include ports 139 (workstation verification), 445 (workstation verification and event log polling), 389 (LDAP), and 445 and 636 (LDAPS).

Key troubleshooting tips include:
- Configure traffic shaping to have a minimum guaranteed bandwidth of 64 Kbps for each domain controller. If there is insufficient bandwidth, some FSSO information might not reach FortiGate.
- Never set the workstation verify interval to 0. This prevents the collector agent from deleting stale entries, which can be especially dangerous in environments where FSSO and non-FSSO users share the same DHCP pool.
- Ensure DNS is configured correctly and is updating IP addresses, if workstation IP addresses change.
- When using passive authentication only, include the group of guest users in a policy and give them access. SSO_Guest_User and active authentication are mutually exclusive.

![FSSO monitoring and troubleshooting](diagram:0)

## Logging Configuration

FSSO-related log messages are generated from authentication events. These include user login and logout events, and NTLM authentication events. To ensure you log all the events needed, set the minimum log level to Notification or Information. The closer the log level is to Debug level, the more information is logged.

The Logging section of the FSSO collector agent allows the following configurations:
- **Debug**: The most detailed log level. Use it when actively troubleshooting issues.
- **Information**: Includes details about login events and workstation checks. This is the recommended level for most troubleshooting.
- **Warning**: The default level. It provides information about failures.
- **Error**: Lists only the most severe events.

You can also enable **Log login events in separate logs** to record user login-related information separately from other logs. The information in this log includes: data received from DC agents, user login/logout information, workstation IP change information, and data sent to FortiGate devices.

## Diagnostic CLI Commands

FortiGate provides several CLI commands for FSSO troubleshooting:

- **`diagnose debug authd fsso list`**: Displays the list of FSSO users that are currently logged in, including the user name, user group, IP address, and the name of the workstation from which they logged in.
- **`execute fsso refresh`**: Manually refreshes user group information from any directory service servers connected to FortiGate, using the collector agent.
- **`diagnose debug authd fsso server-status`**: Shows the status of communication between FortiGate and each collector agent.
- **`diagnose debug fsso-polling detail`**: Displays status information and statistics related to the polls done by FortiGate on each DC in agentless polling. If the read log offset is incrementing, FortiGate is connecting to and reading the logs on the domain controller.
- **`diagnose debug fsso-polling refresh-user`**: Flushes information about all the active FSSO users.
- **`diagnose debug application fssod -1`**: Enables agentless polling mode real-time debug. The fssod daemon handles polling mode on FortiGate.

In agentless polling mode, FortiGate frequently polls the event viewer to get the login events. You can sniff this traffic on port 445. If the read log offset is incrementing but you are not getting any login events, check that the group filter is correct and that the domain controller is creating the correct event IDs.

> **Key terms:** SSO_Guest_User and active authentication are mutually exclusive in FSSO configuration.

> **Key terms:** SSO (Single Sign-On) guest users and active authentication are mutually exclusive in FSSO.

title: How FortiGate uses certificates
content:
## Overview

A digital certificate is a file or password used to authenticate a device, server, or user through cryptography and public key infrastructure (PKI). It is a digital document produced and signed by a CA. Certificates serve three primary purposes:

- **Authentication**: The common name (CN) or subject alternative name (SAN) field, or both, are used to identify the device that the certificate is representing.
- **Encryption and decryption**: Private and public key pairs are used to encrypt and decrypt traffic.
- **Integrity**: Messages are hashed using a secret key known to both the sender and the receiver. The receiver uses the key to check the hash value and confirm the integrity and authenticity of the message data.

FortiGate supports the X.509v3 certificate standard, which is the most common standard for certificates. FortiGate identifies the device or person by reading the CN value in the Subject field, which is expressed as a distinguished name (DN). FortiGate can also use alternate identifiers shown in the Subject Alternative Name field.

![How FortiGate uses certificates](diagram:0)

## How FortiGate Uses Certificates

FortiGate uses digital certificates in multiple areas:

- **Inspection**: FortiGate uses digital certificates for inspection, mainly outbound or inbound traffic inspection. If FortiGate trusts the certificate, it permits the connection. But if FortiGate does not trust the certificate, it can prevent the connection.
- **Privacy**: Certificates, and their associated private keys, ensure that FortiGate can establish a private SSL connection to another service, such as FortiGuard, or a web browser or web server.
- **Authentication**: Users who have certificates issued by a known and trusted CA can authenticate on FortiGate to access the network or establish a VPN connection. Administrator users can use certificates as a second-factor authentication credential to log in to FortiGate.

## Certificate Validation Process

FortiGate runs the following checks before it trusts the certificate:

- Checks the certificate revocation lists (CRL) locally on FortiGate to verify if the certificate has been revoked by the CA. FortiGate can download the relevant CRL and check if the serial number of the certificate is listed.
- Reads the value in the Issuer field to determine if it has the corresponding CA certificate. Without the CA certificate, FortiGate does not trust the certificate.
- Verifies that the current date is between the Valid From and Valid To values. If it is not, the certificate is rendered invalid.
- Validates the signature on the certificate. The signature must be successfully validated.

## Digital Signature Verification

When the CA generates a digital signature, it runs the content of the certificate through a hash function, producing a hash result. The CA signs the original hash result using its private key. The signed hash result is the digital signature.

When validating a certificate, FortiGate:
1. Runs the certificate through a hash function, producing a fresh hash result using the same hashing algorithm identified in the certificate.
2. Verifies the digital signature using the CA public key and the same asymmetric algorithm that the CA used to sign the hash result.
3. Compares the fresh hash result to the original hash result. If the two values are identical, then the integrity of the certificate is confirmed.

If the verification succeeds, it proves that the CA's private key signed the certificate. The terms sign and verify more accurately describe digital signature processes because the purpose of digital signatures is to identify the signer, verify the integrity of the data, and sometimes to inextricably bind the data to the signer.

> **Key terms:** The Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field provides alternate identifiers such as a network ID or an email address.

questionPool.q: What key does FortiGate use to verify a digital signature?

title: Understanding and configuring full SSL inspection and certificate inspection
content:
## Overview

While there are benefits to using HTTPS, there are risks associated with its use because encrypted traffic can be used to get around normal defenses. For example, if a session is encrypted when you download a file containing a virus, the virus might get past your network security measures. You can use full SSL inspection, also known as deep inspection, to inspect encrypted sessions.

There are two SSL inspection modes:

- **SSL certificate inspection**: FortiGate is not decrypting the traffic. During the SSL handshake, FortiGate parses the server name indication (SNI) from the client Hello. The SNI tells FortiGate the hostname of the SSL server. The only security features you can apply using SSL certificate inspection mode are web filtering and application control. Note that certificate inspection does not allow FortiGate to inspect the flow of encrypted data.
- **Full SSL inspection (deep inspection)**: FortiGate performs this inspection by proxying the SSL connection. Two SSL sessions are established—client-to-FortiGate and FortiGate-to-server. This allows FortiGate to encrypt and decrypt packets using its own keys, which allows FortiGate to fully inspect all data inside the encrypted packets.

![Understanding and configuring full SSL inspection and certificate inspection](diagram:0)

## Configuring SSL Inspection Profiles

On FortiGate, you can select the inspection mode applied at the firewall policy level. Three predefined SSL/SSH inspection profiles are available:

- **no-inspection**: The profile applied by default when you create a new firewall policy.
- **certificate-inspection**: Read-only predefined profile for certificate inspection.
- **deep-inspection**: Read-only predefined profile that applies full SSL inspection to outbound traffic.

The predefined certificate-inspection and deep-inspection profiles are read-only. If you want to adjust the profile parameters, you can use the predefined custom-deep-inspection profile or create a new, user-defined profile. When you define a custom SSL/SSH profile, you can enable SSL inspection for outbound traffic with the parameter **Multiple Clients Connecting to Multiple Servers**, or for inbound traffic with the parameter **Protecting SSL Server**.

By default, FortiGate uses the preloaded Fortinet_CA_SSL certificate for traffic reencryption between FortiGate and the destination.

## Certificate Actions and Exemptions

FortiGate can detect certificates that are invalid for these reasons: Expired, Revoked (based on CRL information), Validation timeout, or Validation failed. When a certificate fails, you can configure the following actions:

- **Keep Untrusted & Allow**: FortiGate allows the website and lets the browser decide the action to take.
- **Block**: FortiGate blocks the content of the site.
- **Trust & Allow**: FortiGate allows the website and takes the certificate as trusted.

When FortiGate receives a trusted SSL certificate, it generates a temporary certificate signed by the built-in Fortinet_CA_SSL certificate. When it detects an untrusted certificate (with Allow configured), it generates a temporary certificate signed by Fortinet_CA_Untrusted. For full SSL inspection to work without browser warnings, you must import the Fortinet_CA_SSL certificate into the trusted root CA certificate store of your browser. The Fortinet_CA_Untrusted certificate must not be imported.

Within the full SSL inspection profile, you can also specify which SSL sites to exempt from SSL inspection. The predefined deep-inspection and custom-deep-inspection profiles exclude some web categories—Finance and Banking, and Health and Wellness—and some FQDN addresses. Performing SSL inspection on a site that is enabled with HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) can cause problems with traffic, because browsers that use HSTS refuse to proceed when FortiGate presents a temporary SSL certificate.

## SSL Inspection Requirements and Application Impact

To perform full SSL inspection, FortiGate acts as a web proxy and must act as a CA to reencrypt traffic. The CA certificate used for reencryption must have the extensions: `cA set to True` and `keyUsage set to keyCertSign`. All FortiGate devices come with the self-signed Fortinet_CA_SSL certificate for full SSL inspection.

When enabling SSL inspection, you need to consider the potential impact on SSL-based applications:
- Microsoft Outlook 365 for Windows reports a certificate error when you enable full SSL inspection because the CA certificate used by FortiGate is not trusted.
- Applications with certificate pinning, such as Dropbox, will stop working and must be exempted from SSL inspection.
- SSL inspection applies to other SSL-based protocols such as FTPS, POP3S, SMTPS, STARTTLS, LDAPS, and SIP TLS.

To perform SSL inspection on traffic flowing through FortiGate, you must allow the traffic with a firewall policy and apply an SSL inspection profile to the policy. An SSL inspection profile alone will not trigger a security inspection—you must combine it with other security profiles like Antivirus, Web Filter, Application Control, or IPS.

title: Antivirus basics
content:
## Overview

FortiGate's antivirus engine protects your network by detecting and stopping viruses that could harm your systems or compromise connected devices. Antivirus can run on individual endpoints via FortiClient, or as an inspection engine inside the FortiGate next generation firewall (NGFW). The engine leverages signature databases continuously updated by the FortiGuard antivirus service in real time.

![Antivirus basics](diagram:0)

## Detection Techniques

FortiGate uses several scanning techniques to identify malware:

- **Antivirus scan**: The first, fastest, and simplest method. Detects viruses that are an exact match for a signature in the antivirus database.
- **Grayware scan**: Detects unsolicited programs, known as grayware, installed without the user's knowledge or consent. Often detected using a simple FortiGuard grayware signature.
- **AI scan**: The AI-based scan engine integrates with regular antivirus scanning to detect zero-day malware in Windows portable executable (PE) files. Zero-day malware are new, unknown malware with no existing associated signature. Files detected by the AI scanner are identified with the **W32/AI.Pallas.Suspicious** virus signature.

When all antivirus features are enabled, FortiGate applies scanning in this order: antivirus scan, followed by grayware scan, followed by AI scan.

## Protection Techniques

FortiGate supports several industry-standard antivirus protection techniques:

- **Signature-based detection**: Compares files against the virus signatures database using content pattern recognition language (CPRL), which is more efficient and accurate than traditional methods.
- **Virus outbreak prevention**: The FortiGuard Virus Outbreak Protection Service (VOS) subsidizes the antivirus database with third-party malware hash signatures from FortiGuard's Global Threat Intelligence database. A valid FortiGuard outbreak prevention license is required.
- **External malware block list**: FortiGate can link dynamic external malware block lists hosted on web servers via HTTP/HTTPS URLs. Hash lists can contain MD5, SHA1, and SHA256 hashes.
- **EMS threat feed**: FortiGate receives malware feeds from FortiClient EMS. When EMS threat feed, external malware blocklist, and FortiGuard outbreak prevention are all enabled, the checking order is: antivirus local database, EMS threat feed, external malware blocklist, then FortiGuard outbreak prevention database.
- **CDR (Content Disarm and Reconstruction)**: Sanitizes Microsoft Office documents and PDF files by removing active content such as hyperlinks, embedded media, JavaScript, and macros. CDR supports HTTP, SMTP, POP3, and IMAP. CDR does not support flow-based inspection modes.
- **Behavior-based detection**: Submits suspected malicious files to FortiSandbox for inspection.

## Inspection Modes

FortiGate antivirus can operate in two inspection modes:

- **Flow-based inspection**: Takes a snapshot of content packets and uses pattern matching. It is the default mode. It can be offloaded to CP8 or CP9 processors, and models supporting NTurbo can accelerate antivirus processing to enhance performance.
- **Proxy-based inspection**: Reconstructs content that passes through FortiGate before inspecting it. Provides more feature configuration options including support for MAPI, SSH, and CDR sanitization. If security is your priority, proxy-based inspection mode with client comforting disabled is more appropriate.

Both modes use the full antivirus database (extended or extreme, depending on the CLI command `use-extreme-db` and the FortiGate model) and provide similar detection rates.

> **Key terms:** NTurbo creates a special data path to redirect traffic from the ingress interface to the IPS engine for flow-based antivirus processing.

> **Key terms:** The IPS engine caches the URL of an infected file so a block replacement message is sent on a second access attempt.
