title: Troubleshooting common antivirus issues
content:
## Overview

Effective antivirus troubleshooting on FortiGate requires understanding the available logging tools, update mechanisms, and common configuration pitfalls. When an antivirus profile is applied to at least one firewall policy, you have access to detailed logs and diagnostic commands that help identify and resolve issues quickly.

![Troubleshooting common antivirus issues](diagram:0)

## Logging and Monitoring

Logging is an important part of managing a secure network. When you enable unified threat management (UTM) logging in a firewall policy, you can find details on the AntiVirus log page under Security Events.

When the antivirus scan detects a virus, by default it creates a log that includes:

- Which virus was detected
- The action taken
- The policy ID
- The antivirus profile name
- The detection type
- A link to more information on the FortiGuard website

When you enable oversized file logging, a log entry is created with the message **"Size limit is exceeded"**.

You can also view log details on the **Forward Traffic** page, where firewall policies record traffic activity. The Security dashboard provides another view of relevant information regarding threats to your network, organizing data by source and destination and allowing you to drill down to session log details. You can add the **Advanced Threat Protection Statistics** widget to the dashboard for monitoring purposes.

## Troubleshooting FortiGuard Updates

Viruses are constantly evolving and you must have the latest antivirus definitions version to ensure correct protection. With a valid license, FortiGate checks regularly for updates. If an antivirus profile is applied on at least one firewall policy, you can force an update of the antivirus definitions database with the CLI command `execute update-av`.

If you are having issues with the antivirus license or FortiGuard updates, start troubleshooting with basic connectivity tests. Most of the time, issues related to updates are caused by connectivity problems with FortiGuard servers. You can do the following:

- Make sure that FortiGate has a stable internet connection and can resolve DNS (`update.fortinet.net`).
- If there is another firewall between FortiGate and the internet, make sure TCP port 443 is open and traffic is allowed from and to FortiGate.
- If you continue to see issues with the update, run the real-time debug command to identify the problem.

## Troubleshooting Configuration Issues

If you have a valid contract and updated database but are still having issues catching viruses, start troubleshooting for basic configuration errors. Most of the time, issues are caused by misconfiguration on the device. You can do the following to verify:

- Make sure that the correct antivirus profile is applied on the correct firewall policy.
- Make sure that the correct protocol port is configured when proxy-based inspection mode is used.
- Make sure that you are using the correct antivirus profile and SSL/SSH inspection on all firewall policies.

## Diagnostic Commands

To troubleshoot further, use these CLI commands:

- `get system performance status` — Displays statistics for the last one minute.
- `diagnose antivirus database-info` — Displays current antivirus database information.
- `diagnose autoupdate versions` — Displays current antivirus engine and signature versions.
- `diagnose antivirus test "get scantime"` — Displays scan times for infected files.

title: Understanding inspection modes
content:
## Overview

FortiGate web filtering helps stop infections from malware sites and prevent communication if an infection occurs. After a TCP connection is established, the user requests the content of a specific website using an HTTP GET request. FortiGate checks the HTTP GET request and sends a real-time request to the FortiGuard servers to determine the category of the website. Based on the category information from the FortiGuard Distribution Network (FDN), FortiGate performs a specific action based on the profile applied to the policy.

In FortiOS, there are three main components of web filtering:

- **Web content filtering**: blocks web pages containing words or patterns that you specify.
- **URL filtering**: uses URLs and URL patterns to block or exempt web pages from specific sources, or block malicious URLs discovered by FortiSandbox.
- **FortiGuard Web Filtering service**: provides many additional categories you can use to filter web traffic.

![Understanding inspection modes](diagram:0)

## SSL Certificate Inspection

For encrypted protocols, FortiGate requires additional inspection. When using SSL certificate inspection, FortiGate inspects the headers up to only the SSL/TLS layer. FortiGate does not decrypt or inspect any encrypted traffic — it inspects only the initial unencrypted SSL handshake.

During the TLS handshake, the Client Hello message includes the Server Name Indication (SNI). If the SNI field exists, FortiGate uses it to obtain the FQDN to rate the site. If the SNI is not present, FortiGate retrieves the FQDN from the CN field of the server certificate.

In some cases, the CN server name might not match the requested FQDN. For example, the common name (CN) field in the digital certificate of youtube.com is google.com. So, if FortiGate uses SSL certificate inspection and the browser does not support SNI, FortiGate may incorrectly categorize the site.

## Flow-Based vs. Proxy-Based Inspection

You can configure web filtering in **flow-based** or **proxy-based** inspection mode.

**Flow-based inspection** examines the file as it passes through FortiGate, without buffering it. Packets are analyzed and forwarded as they are received, without waiting for the complete file or web page.

Advantages of flow-based inspection mode:

- The user sees a faster response time for HTTP requests compared to proxy-based inspection mode.
- There is less chance of a time-out error caused by the server at the other end responding slowly.
- From FortiOS 7.4.4 and later, flow-based web filter profiling supports safe search and restrictions on YouTube and Vimeo access.

Disadvantages of flow-based inspection mode:

- A number of security features available in proxy-based inspection mode are not available in flow-based mode.
- Fewer actions are available based on the categorization of the website by FortiGuard services.

**Proxy-based inspection** refers to a transparent proxy. FortiGate buffers traffic and examines it as a whole before determining an action. Because FortiGate examines the data as a whole, it can examine more points of data than in flow-based inspection. The proxy analyzes the headers and may change them, such as HTTP host and URL, for web filtering. If a security profile decides to block the connection, the proxy can send a replacement message to the client. This adds latency to the overall transmission speed.

Make sure that both an SSL inspection profile (such as the certificate-inspection profile) and a web filter profile are selected in the associated firewall policy.

title: Web filtering configuration
content:
## Overview

FortiGate has a read-only preconfigured profile for SSL certificate inspection named **certificate-inspection**. If you want to enable SSL certificate inspection, select this profile when configuring a firewall policy. Alternatively, you can create your own SSL/SSH inspection profile. When configuring the Server certificate SNI check:

- **Enable**: FortiGate uses the domain in the CN field instead of the SNI field if there is a mismatch.
- **Strict**: FortiGate closes the client connection if there is a mismatch between SNI and CN/SAN fields.
- **Disable**: FortiGate always rates URLs based on the FQDN.

You can configure the web filter profile to use a feature set for **proxy-based** or **flow-based** inspection modes. Depending on the mode you select, the available settings are different. Flow-based inspection has fewer available options.

![Web filtering configuration](diagram:0)

## FortiGuard Category Filtering

FortiGuard category filtering enhances the web filter features. Rather than block or allow websites individually, it looks at the category that a website has been rated with. FortiGate then takes action based on that category, not based on the URL.

FortiGuard category filtering is a **live service** that requires an active contract. If the contract expires, there is a two-day grace period during which you can renew before the service ends. After the grace period, FortiGate reports a rating error for every rating request made and, by default, blocks those web pages. You can change this behavior by enabling the **Allow websites when a rating error occurs** setting.

You can configure FortiManager to act as a local FortiGuard server by downloading the databases to FortiManager and configuring FortiGate to validate categories against FortiManager instead of FortiGuard.

The available category actions are:

- **Allow**: permits access but does not create a web filter security log.
- **Monitor**: allows access and creates a security log for analysis purposes.
- **Block**: prevents access and creates a web filter security log. Users get a replacement message.
- **Warning**: informs users that the requested website is not allowed, but gives them the option to proceed. You can customize the warning interval and the warning replacement message.
- **Authenticate**: blocks the requested website unless the user enters a valid username and password. FortiGate supports local and remote authentication using LDAP, RADIUS, and others. You can also customize the interval of time to allow access.

Quotas allow daily access for a specific length of time or bandwidth. At midnight, quotas reset. Once the daily quota is reached for a category, FortiGate blocks the traffic and displays a replacement message page. You can apply quotas to Monitor, Warning, and Authenticate actions.

## Static URL Filtering and Inspection Order

Static URL filtering provides more granularity. Configured URLs in the URL filter are checked from top to bottom against the visited websites. If FortiGate finds a match, it applies the configured action. The four available actions are:

- **Exempt**: allows the traffic from trusted sources to bypass all security inspections.
- **Block**: denies the attempt and the user receives a replacement message.
- **Allow**: permits access. Traffic is passed to remaining operations including FortiGuard web filter, web content filter, and antivirus scanning.
- **Monitor**: allows traffic while creating log entries. Traffic is still subject to all other security profile inspections.

URL filtering supports three pattern types: Simple, Regular Expressions, and Wildcard.

When multiple web filtering features are enabled, the inspection order is:

1. The local static URL filter
2. FortiGuard category filtering (to determine a rating)
3. Advanced filters (such as safe search or removing Active X components)

For each step, if there is no match, FortiGate moves on to the next enabled check.

> **Key terms:** FortiGuard Web Filtering rates URLs by domain and IP address.

> **Key terms:** FortiOS no longer supports proxy-related features in newer inspection modes.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
## Overview

Category-based filtering requires a live connection to FortiGuard. You can verify the connection to FortiGuard servers by running the `diagnose debug rating` CLI command. This command displays a list of FortiGuard servers you can connect to, along with the following information:

- **Weight**: based on the difference in time zones between FortiGate and the server, to reduce the possibility of using a remote server.
- **RTT**: Return Trip Time.
- **Flags**: D (IP returned from DNS), I (Contract server contacted), T (being timed), F (failed).
- **TZ**: Server time zone.
- **FortiGuard-requests**: the number of requests sent by FortiGate to FortiGuard.
- **Curr Lost**: current number of consecutive lost FortiGuard requests (resets to 0 when one packet succeeds).
- **Total Lost**: total number of lost FortiGuard requests.

![Troubleshooting](diagram:0)

## Connectivity and Performance

By default, FortiGate enforces the use of **HTTPS port 443** to perform live filtering with FortiGuard or FortiManager. When the `fortiguard-anycast` command is enabled, the FortiGuard domain name resolves to a single anycast IP address, which is the only entry in the list of FortiGuard servers.

By disabling the FortiGuard anycast setting on the CLI, other ports and protocols become available:

- HTTPS port 53 and port 8888
- UDP port 443, port 53, and port 8888

If you are using UDP port 53, any kind of inspection may reveal that this traffic is not DNS and prevent the service from working. In this case, you can switch to the alternate UDP port 443 or port 8888, or change the protocol to HTTPS. Note that these ports are not guaranteed to be open in all networks, so you must verify beforehand.

If the number of FortiGuard requests is too high, you can enable **Web Filter cache**. Once enabled, FortiGate maintains a list of recent website rating responses in memory. If the URL is already known, FortiGate does not send a rating request. Caching responses reduces the amount of time it takes to establish a rating for a website, since the memory lookup is much quicker than packets travelling on the internet.

## Common Misconfiguration Issues

If you have a live connection to FortiGuard and configured your security profiles, but they are not performing web inspection, most issues are caused by misconfiguration on the device. Verify the following:

- Make sure that the **SSL Inspection field** includes at least one profile with an SSL certification inspection method.
- Make sure that the **correct web filter profile** is applied on the firewall policy.
- Verify the **inspection mode setting** with the feature set in the corresponding web filter profile.

To confirm the correct configuration and web filtering behavior, you can view the **web filter logs**. Log entries include information about the FortiGuard quota and category (if enabled), which web filter profile was used to inspect the traffic, the URL, and more details about the event. You can also view the raw log data by clicking the download icon — the file downloaded is a plaintext file in syslog format.

title: IPS configuration
content:
## Overview

Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) detects network attacks and prevents threats from compromising the network, including protected devices. IPS utilizes signatures, protocol decoders, heuristics, threat intelligence such as FortiGuard Labs, and advanced threat detection to prevent exploitation of known and unknown zero-day threats. FortiGate IPS can perform deep packet inspection to scan encrypted payloads to detect and prevent threats.

![IPS configuration](diagram:0)

## IPS Components

IPS on FortiGate is built on three core components:

- **IPS Signatures**: FortiGate uses signature databases to detect known attacks like exploits. Rate-based IPS signatures detect anomalies such as higher-than-usual CPU use or network traffic. They are part of behavioral analysis, detecting symptoms of new, never-previously-seen attacks.
- **Protocol Decoders**: Parse each packet according to protocol specifications to detect network errors and protocol anomalies. If traffic doesn't conform to the specification—for example, sending malformed or invalid commands to servers—the protocol decoder detects the error.
- **IPS Engine**: Responsible for IPS and protocol decoders, in addition to application control, flow-based antivirus protection, web filtering, and email filtering.

## IPS Sensors and Actions

A FortiGate IPS sensor is a collection of IPS signatures and filters. Multiple sets of signatures, filters, or both may be present in an IPS sensor. Signatures can be added individually or via filters based on attributes like target, severity, protocol, OS, and application.

Predefined IPS sensors include: `default`, `all_default`, `protect_client`, `protect_http_server`, and others. FortiGate downloads a FortiGuard IPS package and new signatures appear in the signature list.

Available actions for IPS signatures:

- **Allow**: Allow traffic to continue to its destination
- **Monitor**: Allow traffic and log the activity
- **Block**: Silently drop traffic matching the signature
- **Reset**: Generate a TCP RST packet when the signature is triggered
- **Quarantine**: Quarantine the attacker's IP address for a set duration
- **Default**: Use the default action of the signatures

When you enable **Packet logging**, FortiGate stores a local copy of the packet that matches the signature, enhancing the view of erroneous or suspicious packets.

## Applying IPS to Firewall Policies

To apply an IPS sensor, you must enable IPS and select the sensor in a firewall policy. For maximum benefit from IPS features, you must use an SSL inspection profile, usually deep-inspection, to parse encrypted payloads.

Filter and signature order matters: the IPS engine evaluates filters and signatures at the top of the list first and applies the first match. Position the most likely matching filters at the top. Avoid too many filters or very large signature groups to reduce CPU and RAM usage.

For false-positive outbreaks, you can add the triggered signature individually and set the action to Monitor while investigating. You can also configure **IP exemptions** to temporarily bypass specific source or destination IP addresses from specific signatures.

For botnet protection, enable botnet scanning on the IPS profile. Botnet and C&C actions include Disable, Block, or Monitor.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
## Overview

Troubleshooting IPS on FortiGate involves reviewing logs, diagnosing CPU issues, and managing fail-open scenarios. By identifying, investigating, and managing common issues with IPS deployments, you can maintain effective network security while minimizing disruptions.

![Troubleshooting](diagram:0)

## Reviewing IPS Logs

IPS logs are available on the **Security Events** pane on the **Log & Report** page. You can view the logs by clicking on **Intrusion Prevention**. If you enabled security events logging in the firewall policies that apply IPS, those logs are captured automatically.

You should review IPS logs frequently. The logs are an important source of information about the kinds of attacks being targeted at your network. This helps you develop action plans and focus on specific events, for example, patching a critical vulnerability.

## Diagnosing High CPU Usage

Short spikes in CPU usage by IPS processes can be caused by firewall policy or profile changes. These spikes are usually normal. However, continuous high CPU use by the IPS engines is not normal and should be investigated.

Use the `diagnose test application ipsmonitor` command with the following options:

- **Option 1**: Check the current status of the IPS engines
- **Option 2**: Disable the IPS engine completely (use again to restore IPS inspection)
- **Option 5**: Enable IPS bypass mode — the IPS engine is still running but not inspecting traffic
- **Option 99**: Restart the IPS — guarantees all IPS-related processes restart correctly

If CPU use decreases after enabling IPS bypass mode (option 5), it usually indicates that the volume of traffic being inspected is too high for that FortiGate model. If CPU use remains high after enabling IPS bypass mode, it usually indicates a problem in the IPS engine, which you must report to Fortinet support.

## Managing IPS Fail-Open

IPS goes into fail-open mode when the IPS socket buffer is full for new packets. The IPS engine has no space in memory to create more sessions and must decide whether to drop or bypass sessions without inspection.

- **Fail-open enabled**: Some new packets will pass through without being inspected, depending on system load
- **Fail-open disabled** (default): New packets are dropped

IPS fail-open is recommended only in situations where network availability takes precedence over network security, such as in a datacenter.

When troubleshooting fail-open scenarios:

- Identify patterns: Has traffic volume increased recently? Have throughput demands increased? Does fail-open trigger at specific times during the day?
- Tune and optimize your IPS configuration: Create IPS profiles specific to the type of traffic being inspected
- Disable IPS profiles on policies that don't need them to free up resources

> **Key terms:** When IPS fail-open is disabled, new packets are dropped if the IPS engine is unavailable.

title: Application control basics
content:
## Overview

Application control on FortiGate identifies and controls network applications regardless of the port or protocol they use. Because application control uses the IPS engine, which uses flow-based inspection, the inspection is always flow-based. You can configure application control in proxy-based and flow-based firewall policies.

![Application control basics](diagram:0)

## How Application Control Works

Application control identifies applications, such as Google Talk, by matching known patterns to the application transmission patterns. An application can be accurately identified only if its transmission pattern is unique. However, not every application behaves in a unique way. Many applications reuse pre-existing, standard protocols and communication methods.

For example, many video games, such as World of Warcraft, use the BitTorrent protocol to distribute game patches. With the help of the IPS engine, application control analyzes network traffic and detects application traffic, even if the application is using standard or non-standard protocols and ports. It doesn't operate using built-in protocol states. As a consequence, application control is better suited for detecting P2P protocols, because they use port randomization, pinholes, and changing encryption pattern techniques.

## Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Protocols

Peer-to-peer (P2P) downloads divide each file among multiple (theoretically unlimited) peers. Each peer delivers part of the file. As the number of peers increases to n, the file is delivered n times faster. This is unlike traditional client-server architecture, where popularity could effectively cause a denial of service (DoS) attack on the server.

Some software, such as BitTorrent distributions of Linux and games distributing new patches, leverage this advantage. Even if each client has little bandwidth, together they can offer more bandwidth for the download than many powerful servers. Because the protocols are usually evasive, and there will be many sessions to many peers, P2P protocols are difficult to completely block.

## Hierarchical Signature Database

The FortiGuard application control signature database is organized in a hierarchical structure. This gives you the ability to inspect traffic with more granularity. Many web applications offer functionality that can be embedded in third-party websites or applications. For example, you can embed a Meta Like button at the end of an article, or reference a YouTube video on an educational website.

FortiOS gives administrators all the tools they need to inspect subapplication traffic. You can block Meta applications while allowing users to collaborate using Meta chat. After FortiGate downloads a FortiGuard Application Control Signature package, new signatures appear in the signature list, organized by category and hierarchical structure.

title: Application control feature configuration and monitoring
content:
## Overview

For each filter in the application control profile, you must indicate an action — what FortiGate does when traffic matches. The available actions are:

- **Allow**: passes the traffic and does not generate a log.
- **Monitor**: passes the traffic, but also generates a log message.
- **Block**: drops the detected traffic and generates a log message.
- **Quarantine**: blocks the traffic from the suspected source until the expiration time is reached, and generates a log message.

If you are not sure which action to choose, **Monitor** can be useful initially while you study your network. After you have studied your network traffic, you can fine-tune your filter selection by choosing the most appropriate action. If an application requires feedback to prevent instability or other unwanted behavior, you might choose Quarantine instead of Block. Otherwise, the most efficient use of FortiGate resources is to block.

![Application control feature configuration and monitoring](diagram:0)

## Additional Options and Block Pages

The application sensor provides additional options:

- **Network Protocol Enforcement**: allows you to configure network services (for example, FTP, HTTP, and HTTPS) on known ports (for example, 21, 80, and 443), while blocking those services on other ports. If a protocol dissector confirms the service of network traffic, Network Protocol Enforcement checks whether the confirmed service is allowlisted under the server port — if not, it is a violation and IPS can take the configured action.
- **Block applications detected on non-default ports**: FortiGate compares the ports used by the application with the ones defined in FortiGuard application signatures. The traffic is blocked if it does not match.
- **Replacement Messages for HTTP-based Applications**: allows you to replace blocked content from HTTP/HTTPS applications with an explanation for the user's benefit. For non-HTTP/HTTPS applications, FortiGate only drops the packets or resets the TCP connection.

For HTTP-based applications, application control can provide a **block page** explaining why the application was blocked. If deep inspection is enabled in the firewall policy, all HTTPS-based applications also provide this block page. The block page contains:

- Signature that detected the application
- Signature category
- URL that was specifically blocked
- User name and group name (if authentication is enabled)
- Universal unique identifier (UUID) of the policy governing the traffic

The UUID helps identify which policy on FortiGate blocked the page, even across a large number of policies and FortiGate devices.

## Scan Order, Priority, and Monitoring

After the IPS engine examines the traffic stream for a signature match, FortiGate scans packets for matches in this order:

1. **Application and filter overrides**: If you have configured application or filter overrides, the application control profile considers those first, starting at the top of the list — like firewall policies.
2. **Categories**: The application control profile then applies the action configured for applications in the selected categories.

The priority in which application and filter overrides are placed takes precedence. For example, if a filter override (such as Excessive-Bandwidth) is placed above an application override, the filter override action applies first — even for applications that are set to Monitor in the overrides section.

After you configure an application control profile, you must apply it to a **firewall policy**. When you enable the logging of security events or all sessions on a firewall policy, application control events are also logged.

You can monitor application control events in:

- **Log & Report > Security Events > Application Control**: shows all application control events with details on source, destination, application, and action.
- **Forward Traffic logs**: also records activity governed by the firewall policy. Use the Policy ID or Policy UUID fields to identify which policy applied application control.
- **Dashboard > FortiView Applications**: shows a summary of traffic matched by application control. Select a specific application to drill down into session and bytes information.

> **Key terms:** Application control can monitor the user's browser history and track web application usage.

> **Key terms:** Dailymotion is blocked because the filter override is checked first and Dailymotion uses excessive bandwidth.

title: IPsec basics
content:
## Overview

IPsec is a vendor-neutral set of standard protocols used to join two physically distinct LANs. The LANs are joined as if they were a single logical network, despite being separated by the internet. Regardless of the vendor, IPsec VPNs almost always provide three important benefits:

- **Authentication**: to verify the identity of both ends
- **Data integrity (or HMAC)**: to prove that encapsulated data has not been tampered with as it crosses a potentially hostile network
- **Confidentiality (or encryption)**: to make sure that only the intended recipient can read the message

![IPsec basics](diagram:0)

## IPsec Protocol Suite

IPsec is a suite of separate protocols:

- **IKE (Internet Key Exchange)**: used to authenticate peers, exchange keys, and negotiate the encryption and checksums — essentially the control channel. Uses UDP port 500, or UDP port 4500 when NAT-T is enabled.
- **ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload)**: the encrypted payload, which is the data channel
- **AH (Authentication Header)**: provides checksums to verify data integrity but does not offer encryption. FortiGate does not use AH, so the AH IP protocol (51) does not need to be allowed.

IPsec can operate in two encapsulation modes:

- **Transport mode**: directly encapsulates and protects the fourth layer (transport) and above. It does not protect the original IP header and does not add an additional IP header. Used only for end-to-end VPNs.
- **Tunnel mode**: a true tunnel that encapsulates the whole IP packet and adds a new IP header at the beginning.

## IKE Phases and Security Associations

IKE establishes an IPsec VPN tunnel and uses two distinct phases. The SA negotiated during phase 1 is called the **IKE SA**, and the SA negotiated during phase 2 is called the **IPsec SA**.

- FortiGate uses IKE SAs to set up a secure channel to negotiate IPsec SAs
- FortiGate uses IPsec SAs for encrypting and decrypting data through the tunnel
- SAs expire and need to be renegotiated by the peers after they have reached their lifetime

There are two IKE versions: **IKEv1** and **IKEv2**. IKEv2 provides a simpler operation, supports NAT-T natively, and is a more reliable protocol because peers must acknowledge messages exchanged. IKEv1 supports XAuth for additional user authentication, while IKEv2 supports EAP.

## VPN Topologies

Common IPsec deployment topologies include:

- **Remote access VPN**: FortiGate is configured as a dial-up server; the remote user connects using a VPN client like FortiClient. The IP address of the remote user is usually dynamic.
- **Site-to-site (LAN-to-LAN)**: two peers communicate directly to connect two networks at different offices.
- **Hub-and-spoke**: all branch office spokes connect through a central hub FortiGate. Easy to manage, but if the hub fails, VPN failure is company-wide.
- **Full mesh**: every location connects to every other location directly. Less latency but requires each FortiGate to be more powerful and involves more tunnels to configure.
- **Partial mesh**: a compromise between hub-and-spoke and full mesh, minimizing required resources while reducing latency for critical paths.

> **Key terms:** In a hub-and-spoke topology, if the FortiGate at HQ (headquarters) fails, the VPN failure is company-wide.

> **Key terms:** In a full mesh topology with five FortiGate devices, 20 tunnels must be configured in total.

title: IPsec configuration
content:
## Overview

When you create an IPsec tunnel on the GUI, FortiGate redirects you to the IPsec Wizard. The wizard simplifies the creation of the new VPN by walking you through a four to five-step process. The first step is to select a template type: Site to Site, Hub-and-Spoke, Remote Access, or Custom. If you select Custom, FortiGate takes you directly to the phase 1 and phase 2 settings. If you are new to FortiGate, using the IPsec wizard is recommended. Note that this lesson covers only IKEv1 configuration.

![IPsec configuration](diagram:0)

## Phase 1 Configuration

Phase 1 authenticates peers and sets up a secure channel for negotiating IPsec SAs. The GUI breaks phase 1 into four sections: **Network**, **Authentication**, **Phase 1 Proposal**, and **XAUTH**.

Key **Network** settings include:

- **Remote Gateway**: three types — Static IP Address, Dialup User, and Dynamic DNS. Use Dialup User when the remote peer IP is unknown (mobile clients, branch offices with dynamic IPs). Use Static IP Address or Dynamic DNS when you know the remote peer address.
- **Interface**: the interface where the IPsec tunnel terminates on the local FortiGate, usually the WAN interface.
- **Mode Config**: enables automatic IP assignment through IKE. When Remote Gateway is set to Dialup User, FortiGate acts as an IKE mode config server, similar to DHCP — pushing IP address, netmask, and DNS servers to dial-up clients.
- **NAT Traversal**: controls behavior for NAT traversal. When enabled, peers detect any NAT device along the path and switch IKE negotiation to UDP port 4500, encapsulating ESP in UDP port 4500.
- **Dead Peer Detection (DPD)**: detects failed (dead) tunnels. Three DPD modes: On Demand (default), On Idle, and Disabled.

**Authentication** settings:

- **Method**: Pre-shared Key (both peers must share the same key) or Signature (digital certificates, validated by the CA certificate installed on the other peer).
- **Mode**: Main mode (more secure, pre-shared key hash exchanged encrypted, six packets) or Aggressive mode (faster, three packets, but hash exchanged unencrypted). Use aggressive mode when multiple dial-up tunnels terminate on the same FortiGate IP and remote peers use dynamic IP addresses with peer IDs.
- **XAuth**: forces remote users to authenticate additionally with username and password. When Remote Gateway is Dialup User, FortiGate acts as authentication server (PAP Server, CHAP Server, or Auto Server).

**Phase 1 Proposal** settings:

- **Encryption and Authentication algorithms**: select combinations that match your security policy.
- **Diffie-Hellman Groups**: DH is mandatory in phase 1. Higher DH group numbers are more secure but result in longer compute time.
- **Key Lifetime**: defines the IKE SA lifetime; a new IKE SA is negotiated when this expires.

## Phase 2 Configuration

After phase 1 establishes a secure channel, phase 2 negotiates IPsec SAs for encrypting traffic. Key phase 2 concepts:

- **Phase 2 selectors (quick mode selectors)**: define the encryption domain — the traffic you want to protect with IPsec. You specify Local Address and Remote Address. Both peers' selectors must match for point-to-point tunnels.
- Each phase 1 can have **multiple phase 2s** with different selectors.
- **Phase 2 proposals**: define the algorithms for encrypting and decrypting tunnel data. Note that 3DES is more resource-intensive than AES, which may impact IPsec throughput.
- **Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)**: when enabled, FortiGate uses DH to recalculate new secret keys each time phase 2 expires, so new keys are not derived from older keys.
- **Key Lifetime**: can be time-based (Seconds), volume-based (Kilobytes), or Both. When thresholds differ between peers, FortiGate uses the lowest threshold value.
- **Auto-negotiate**: when enabled, FortiGate negotiates new SAs before current SAs expire and starts using new SAs right away, preventing traffic disruption.
- **Hardware offloading**: on supported FortiGate models, IPsec encryption/decryption can be offloaded to NP units for better performance. Algorithms like CHACHA20POLY1305 are not supported for hardware offload.

> **Key terms:** In aggressive mode, the peer ID information is sent in the first packet, allowing FortiGate to match the remote peer with the correct dial-up tunnel.

> **Key terms:** PFS ensures new keys are not derived from older keys, making it harder for an attacker to crack the tunnel.

title: Routing and firewall policies for IPsec VPNs
content:
## Overview

FortiGate supports two types of IPsec VPNs: route-based and policy-based. Policy-based is a legacy implementation supported only for backward compatibility and is not recommended for new deployments. Route-based IPsec VPNs are the standard approach in FortiOS 7.6.

In a route-based IPsec VPN, FortiGate automatically adds a virtual interface with the VPN name. This allows you to configure routing and firewall policies for IPsec traffic the same way you do for non-IPsec traffic. Route-based VPNs also support L2TP-over-IPsec, GRE-over-IPsec, and dynamic routing protocols such as OSPF or BGP for scalability and best path selection.

![Routing and firewall policies for IPsec VPNs](diagram:0)

## Routing Configuration

The routing configuration depends on the type of remote gateway configured:

- **Dialup User with add-route enabled**: FortiGate automatically adds a static route for the remote network after phase 2 comes up. The route is removed if phase 2 goes down.
- **Dialup User with add-route disabled**: FortiGate does not add static routes automatically; a dynamic routing protocol is used between peers.
- **Static IP Address or Dynamic DNS**: You must manually configure static routes, selecting the virtual tunnel interface as the outgoing interface.

## Firewall Policies

You must configure at least one firewall policy that accepts traffic on your IPsec tunnel; otherwise, the tunnel will not come up. Typically, two firewall policies are required:

- **Incoming policy**: allows traffic initiated from the remote site
- **Outgoing policy**: allows traffic initiated from the local network

Both policies are configured using the virtual tunnel interface (phase 1 name) as the incoming or outgoing interface.

## Redundant VPN Configurations

To improve resiliency, you can configure two IPsec VPNs using a second ISP connection. There are two types of redundant VPNs:

- **Partially redundant**: one peer (usually the hub) terminates each VPN on different physical ports; the other peer uses the same port on both VPNs.
- **Fully redundant**: both peers terminate their VPNs on different physical ports, making both sides fault tolerant.

To configure redundancy: create one phase 1 and at least one phase 2 for each path, enable Dead Peer Detection (DPD) on both ends, and configure static routes so the primary VPN has a lower distance (higher preference) than the backup. Configure firewall policies to allow traffic through both primary and backup VPNs.

title: Monitoring and logs
content:
## Overview

FortiGate provides multiple tools to monitor IPsec VPN status, review event logs, and troubleshoot common issues. Understanding these tools enables you to quickly detect problems and restore connectivity. Monitoring covers both the GUI dashboard and the CLI diagnostic commands.

![Monitoring and logs](diagram:0)

## IPsec Widget and GUI Monitoring

On the GUI dashboard, you can use the IPsec widget to monitor the status of your IPsec VPNs. The widget shows the phase 1 and phase 2 status of each VPN and lets you bring up or bring down individual VPNs:

- **Bring up**: you can bring up a particular phase 2 selector or all phase 2 selectors. Bringing up a phase 2 selector also brings up its phase 1 automatically.
- **Bring down**: you can bring down a particular phase 2 selector, all selectors, or the entire tunnel (which brings down all phase 2 selectors and phase 1).
- **VPN status**: the VPN is considered up when at least one phase 2 selector is up. If all phase 2 selectors are down, the VPN status is also down.
- The widget also displays the amount of data sent and received through the tunnel.

For routes: if the remote gateway is Static IP Address or Dynamic DNS, static routes become active in the routing table after phase 1 comes up. For dialup peers, a static route with distance 15 is added after phase 2 comes up and removed when phase 2 goes down.

## VPN Event Logs

FortiGate logs IPsec VPN events by default. To view IPsec VPN event logs, navigate to **Log & Report > System Events > VPN Events**. The logs track:

- Phase 1 and phase 2 negotiation progress
- Tunnel up and tunnel down events
- DPD failures

## CLI Diagnostic Commands

Several CLI commands are available for detailed IPsec diagnostics:

- `diagnose vpn tunnel list` — displays current IPsec SA information for all active tunnels
- `diagnose vpn tunnel list name <tunnel name>` — shows SA information for a specific tunnel
- `get vpn ipsec tunnel details` — provides traffic counters, negotiated quick mode selectors, encryption and authentication parameters
- `diagnose vpn ike gateway list` — provides details about a specific tunnel's IKE gateway
- `diagnose vpn ike gateway clear` — closes a phase 1; use with caution as running it without specifying a phase 1 name clears all phase 1s across all VDOMs

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

Key scenarios and recommended approaches:

- **Tunnel doesn't come up**: use the IKE real-time debug; an error message usually appears indicating the root cause
- **Tunnel is unstable**: DPD packets are typically being lost, which indicates the problem might be on the ISP side
- **Tunnel is up but traffic isn't passing**: use the debug flow; one peer may be dropping packets, routing traffic incorrectly, or the packets don't match the quick mode selectors

title: SD-WAN solution and its use cases
content:
## Overview

Software-defined WAN (SD-WAN) provides dynamic, policy-based, application path selection across multiple WAN connections. The Fortinet implementation is called **secure SD-WAN** because it also provides security by leveraging built-in FortiOS features such as IPsec, link monitoring, advanced routing, internet services database (ISDB), traffic shaping, UTM inspection, and load balancing.

Note that SD-WAN controls **egress traffic**, not ingress traffic. The return traffic may use a different link from the one SD-WAN chose for egress.

![SD-WAN solution and its use cases](diagram:0)

## Key Benefits

- **Effective WAN use**: Combine public links (broadband, LTE) and private links (MPLS) in a hybrid WAN to securely steer traffic to internet, public cloud, private cloud, and the corporate network.
- **Cost reduction**: Steer traffic over low-cost fast internet links more than over high-cost slow private links. MPLS links are often used for critical traffic only or as failover links.
- **Improved application performance**: Steer traffic through the best link that meets application requirements. Use traffic shaping to prioritize sensitive and critical applications during congestion.

## SD-WAN Use Cases

**Direct Internet Access (DIA)** — also known as local breakout — is the most common use case. A site has multiple internet links (underlay links) and FortiGate steers internet traffic across them. Sensitive traffic is sent over best-performing links, while non-critical traffic is distributed using a best-effort approach. Static default routes or BGP are used for routing.

**Site-to-Site VPN** — Companies follow a hub-and-spoke topology using VPN tunnels (typically dynamic IPsec tunnels) as overlay links established over internet or MPLS underlay links. SD-WAN monitors tunnel quality and selects the best performing link. BGP is often used for dynamic routing through the tunnels.

**Remote Internet Access (RIA)** — also known as remote breakout. Internet traffic from spokes is backhauled through the WAN using overlay links and breaks out to the internet at the hub. The main reason for RIA is to centralize security inspection on a high-end hub FortiGate device, reducing costs and administrative overhead at spoke sites. RIA also serves as DIA backup when local internet links degrade.

## Underlay vs. Overlay Links

- **Underlays**: Physical links rented from an ISP (cable, DSL, fiber, MPLS, 3G/4G/5G/LTE). Traffic is restricted to ISP routing policies and is typically unencrypted.
- **Overlays**: Virtual links built on top of underlays, commonly IPsec tunnels. Original packets are encapsulated in ESP packets, freeing networks from ISP routing restrictions and providing privacy and authentication.

title: SD-WAN fundamentals
content:
## Overview

On FortiGate, an SD-WAN configuration is built on **SD-WAN rules**. SD-WAN rules combine traffic matching criteria and traffic steering preferences. The three core building blocks are:

- **Members**: Logical or physical interfaces used to steer traffic.
- **Zones**: Logical groupings of members that share similar firewall policy requirements. FortiGate creates one default zone called `virtual-wan-link`.
- **Performance SLA rules**: Define how to monitor member status and performance criteria such as packet loss, jitter, and latency.

FortiGate evaluates SD-WAN rules top to bottom (first match), similar to firewall policies. If no user-defined rule matches, the **implicit rule** is used, which by default load-balances traffic across all available SD-WAN members.

![SD-WAN fundamentals](diagram:0)

## Members, Zones, and Underlays/Overlays

**Underlays** are physical ISP links (cable, DSL, fiber, MPLS, 3G/4G/5G/LTE). Traffic is subject to ISP routing policies and is typically unencrypted.

**Overlays** are virtual links built on top of underlays, commonly IPsec tunnels. Because packets are encapsulated in ESP, overlay traffic is not restricted to ISP routing policies.

SD-WAN zones allow administrators to group members with similar firewall policy requirements — typically grouping underlays and overlays into separate zones. Firewall policies must reference SD-WAN zones, not individual SD-WAN members.

## Performance SLAs and Strategies

**Performance SLAs** monitor member health actively or passively:
- **Active**: FortiGate sends probes every 500 ms by default to configured beacon servers.
- **Passive**: Health is determined from actual traffic passing through the member.
- **Prefer Passive**: Passive monitoring with active probes as fallback.

Only active monitoring can detect if a link is alive or dead. SLA targets define latency, jitter, and packet loss thresholds.

**Strategies** define preferred member selection:
- **Manual**: Members preferred by configuration order; metrics are not considered.
- **Best quality**: Prefers the best-performing member based on quality criteria.
- **Lowest cost (SLA)**: Prefers the member meeting the configured SLA target; member cost then configuration order are tiebreakers.

Manual and Lowest cost (SLA) strategies can be combined with load balancing to steer traffic through multiple members simultaneously.

## Routing in SD-WAN

SD-WAN rules are essentially policy routes evaluated before the FIB. Key routing principles:

1. SD-WAN rules are skipped if the best route to the destination is not an SD-WAN member.
2. SD-WAN rules are skipped if none of the configured members have a valid route to the destination.
3. The implicit SD-WAN rule equals standard FIB lookup.

When a static route references a zone as the outgoing interface, FortiOS installs a route per member in that zone. Because they share the same distance (default 1), they become **ECMP routes**. Per-member static routes have a default distance of 10.

Firewall policies must allow SD-WAN traffic and must reference SD-WAN zones rather than individual members.

> **Key terms:** SD-WAN rules can match traffic by source IP, destination IP, application, internet service, or ToS.

title: SD-WAN basic monitoring
content:
## Overview

Because of the dynamic nature of SD-WAN routing, you should periodically check the link health, routing behavior, and traffic distribution of your SD-WAN devices. You might want to check that traffic distribution corresponds to expectations — for instance, that only critical traffic is steered through the costliest links. FortiGate provides both general monitoring tools and dedicated SD-WAN GUI monitoring pages.

![SD-WAN basic monitoring](diagram:0)

## GUI Monitoring Tools

The **Network dashboard** is the first place to check SD-WAN behavior. By default it includes three widgets: static and dynamic routing, IPsec tunnels status, and SD-WAN interfaces performances. The **SD-WAN widget** provides an overview of the status of each monitored SD-WAN link. You can click any widget to expand and get additional details. From the detailed view, hover over graphs or click graph segments (such as the red packet-loss portion of the circle) to filter members and display only those matching the selected criteria.

The **SD-WAN Zones page** (Network > SD-WAN) provides a synthetic view of zones and members. Zones with no member appear with a red icon. The diagram at the top displays traffic allocation per interface evaluated by bandwidth, volume, or number of sessions.

The **SD-WAN Rules page** (Network > SD-WAN) provides a summary view of SD-WAN rules, showing main configuration parameters, members in use, and the last time a rule was used to steer traffic. You can reorder rules using drag-and-drop.

## Performance SLA Monitoring

The **Performance SLAs page** shows packet loss, latency, and jitter graphs for each member using the selected SLA. Key behaviors:

- If an SLA target is configured, it appears as a horizontal dotted line on the graph
- Alive members are shown with a green up arrow icon; dead members with a red down arrow icon
- For a missed SLA target, the impacted metric is highlighted in red
- Note that the green up arrows indicate only that the server is responding to the health check — not that all SLA targets are being met
- Graphs are limited to the last minute

You should investigate any prolonged issues with packet loss, latency, or jitter to ensure your network traffic does not experience outages or degraded performance.

## Event Logs and Forward Traffic Logs

The **System Events log summary** (Log & Report > System Events) provides an overview of recent events ordered by category. The **SD-WAN Events** widget reports SLA status changes and priority member order changes. The **VPN Events** widget provides useful information to understand overlay links behavior.

The **SD-WAN Events subsection** on the Events page displays logs reporting state changes of SD-WAN members — for example, a warning that a port changed from alive to dead, followed by logs that the member preference in the corresponding rule was updated.

The **Forward Traffic logs page** is useful to identify how sessions are distributed in SD-WAN and the reason. Enable the **SD-WAN Rule Name** and **SD-WAN Quality** columns (disabled by default). The SD-WAN Rule Name column specifies the matched rule; SD-WAN Quality identifies the member to which the session was steered and the reason. Note that when traffic is steered by the Implicit SD-WAN rule, the SD-WAN Rule Name field remains empty.

## CLI Diagnostics

For CLI-based troubleshooting:

- **Forward traffic logs with verbosity levels 4–6**: view the egress interface using the CLI packet capture tool
- **`diagnose firewall proute list`**: shows policy route entries including `vwl_service` (SD-WAN rule) and `vwl_mbr` (SD-WAN member) fields, rule hit count, and last hit time
- **`diagnose sys session list`**: shows session detail including `sdwan_mbr_seq` (SD-WAN member ID) and `sdwan_service_id` (SD-WAN rule ID)

> **Key terms:** The SD-WAN monitor shows SLA health checks over the past 5 minutes by default.

title: HA operation modes and primary FortiGate election
content:
## Overview

FortiGate High Availability (HA) uses the FortiGate Clustering Protocol (FGCP) to discover members, elect the primary FortiGate, synchronize data among members, and monitor the health of members. FortiGate HA links and synchronizes two or more FortiGate devices to form a cluster for redundancy and performance purposes.

A cluster includes one device that acts as the primary FortiGate. The primary sends its complete configuration to other members that join the cluster, overwriting their configuration (except for a few settings). It synchronizes session information, forwarding information base (FIB) entries, FortiGuard definitions, and other operation-related information to the secondary (standby) devices.

![HA operation modes and primary FortiGate election](diagram:0)

## HA Operation Modes

FortiGate supports two HA operation modes:

**Active-Passive:**
- The primary FortiGate is the only FortiGate that actively processes traffic
- Secondary devices remain in passive mode, monitoring the status of the primary device
- If a problem is detected on the primary FortiGate, one of the secondary devices takes over the primary role (HA failover)
- If a secondary FortiGate fails, the primary updates its list of available secondary devices and monitors for the failed secondary to come back online

**Active-Active:**
- All cluster members can process traffic
- The primary FortiGate can distribute supported sessions to the secondary devices based on HA settings and traffic type
- If a secondary device fails, the primary reassigns sessions to a different secondary FortiGate
- Operation-related data is synchronized between devices in the cluster, as in active-passive mode

## Cluster Requirements

To successfully form an HA cluster, all members must share the same:

- **Model**: hardware model or VM model
- **Firmware version**
- **Licensing**: FortiGuard license, VDOM license, FortiClient license, etc. (the cluster resolves to the lowest licensing level among all members)
- **Hard drive configuration**: same number and size of drives and partitions
- **Operating mode**: NAT mode or transparent mode for the management VDOM

For configuration, each member must have the same group ID, group name, password, and heartbeat interface settings. Configure at least two heartbeat interfaces for redundancy. Heartbeat interfaces should be placed in the same broadcast domain, or connected directly for two-member clusters.

## Primary FortiGate Election (Override Disabled)

When HA override is disabled (the default), the election process evaluates criteria in this order:

1. **Monitored interfaces up**: the member with the most available monitored interfaces becomes primary
2. **HA uptime**: the member with the highest HA uptime (by at least 5 minutes) becomes primary
3. **Priority**: the member with the highest priority becomes primary
4. **Serial number**: the member with the highest serial number becomes primary

The election stops at the first criterion that successfully selects a primary. With override disabled, HA uptime has precedence over priority. To manually fail over to a secondary device, run `diagnose sys ha reset-uptime` on the primary to reset its HA uptime to 0.

## Primary FortiGate Election (Override Enabled)

When HA override is enabled, priority is considered before HA uptime. This lets you designate a preferred primary device by giving it the highest priority. The disadvantage is that when the original primary becomes available again, it triggers a failover to reclaim the primary role. The override setting and device priority values are not synchronized to cluster members — you must manually configure them on each member.

title: Cluster synchronization
content:
## Overview

To prepare for a failover, an HA cluster keeps its configurations in sync. FortiGate HA uses a combination of both incremental and complete synchronizations. Understanding the roles of the primary and secondary members, and what gets synchronized, is key to managing a healthy HA cluster.

![Cluster synchronization](diagram:0)

## Primary FortiGate Tasks

The primary FortiGate has several synchronization and monitoring responsibilities:

- **Cluster monitoring**: broadcasts hello packets and listens for hello packets from other members; members use hello packets to identify whether other FortiGate devices are alive
- **Configuration synchronization**: synchronizes its operation-related data to secondary members, including configuration, FIB entries, DHCP leases, ARP table, FortiGuard definitions, and IPsec tunnel security associations (SAs)
- **Session synchronization** (optional): when enabled, the new primary can resume communication for sessions after a failover event, allowing existing sessions to continue with minimal or no interruption
- **Session distribution** (active-active only): distributes sessions to secondary members

Note that some configuration settings are NOT synchronized because they are device-specific: host name, HA priority, and HA override settings.

## Secondary FortiGate Tasks

Secondary members also broadcast hello packets for discovery and monitoring purposes. In **active-passive mode**, secondary devices act as standby devices: they receive synchronization data but do not process traffic. If the primary fails, the secondary devices elect a new primary.

In **active-active mode**, secondary devices process all traffic assigned to them by the primary device.

Once a cluster is in sync, configuration changes made on any member (primary or secondary) are propagated to all other members. However, it is recommended that you make configuration changes on the primary device to prevent loss of changes if there are synchronization issues.

## Synchronization Process

FortiGate HA uses both complete and incremental synchronization:

- **Complete synchronization**: when a new FortiGate joins the cluster, the primary compares its configuration checksum with the new member's checksum. If checksums don't match, the primary uploads its complete configuration to the secondary.
- **Incremental synchronization**: after the initial sync, whenever a change is made to the configuration of any cluster device, only the change is sent to all other cluster devices over the HA heartbeat link — not the full configuration.

The cluster checks every 60 seconds to ensure all devices are synchronized. If a secondary device is out of sync, its checksum is checked every 15 seconds. If the checksum doesn't match for five consecutive checks, FortiGate performs a complete resynchronization of that secondary device.

## Settings NOT Synchronized

The following configuration settings are not synchronized in HA:

- System interface settings of the HA reserved management interface and its default route
- In-band HA management interface
- HA override
- HA device priority
- Virtual cluster priority
- FortiGate host name
- HA priority setting for a ping server (dead gateway detection)
- All licenses except FortiToken licenses (serial numbers)
- Cache
- GUI dashboard widgets

> **Key terms:** HA cluster members communicate through hello packets broadcasted over the heartbeat interfaces.

A complete synchronization where the primary uploads its full configuration
No synchronization — the new member keeps its own config
Partial synchronization of only critical settings
questionPool.explanation: When a new FortiGate joins the cluster, the primary compares checksums. If the checksums don't match, the primary FortiGate uploads its complete configuration to the secondary FortiGate.

questionPool.question: What type of synchronization sends only changed objects rather than the full configuration?
questionPool.explanation: After the initial synchronization, whenever a change is made to the configuration of an HA cluster device, incremental synchronization sends only the same configuration change to all other cluster devices over the HA heartbeat link.

questionPool.explanation: By default, the cluster checks every 60 seconds to ensure that all devices are synchronized. If a secondary device is out of sync, its checksum is checked every 15 seconds.

questionPool.question: If an out-of-sync secondary device's checksum doesn't match for how many consecutive 15-second checks before a full resync is triggered?
questionPool.explanation: If the checksum of the out-of-sync secondary device doesn't match for five consecutive checks (every 15 seconds), FortiGate performs a complete resynchronization of that secondary device.

questionPool.question: In active-passive mode, what do secondary devices do while the primary is functioning normally?
choices: Process a portion of the traffic
Act as standby devices, receiving synchronization data but not processing traffic
Perform health checks on external servers
questionPool.explanation: In active-passive mode, the secondary devices act as a standby device, receiving synchronization data but not actually processing any traffic.

questionPool.question: What is the benefit of enabling session synchronization in an HA cluster?
choices: It speeds up the primary election process
The new primary can resume communication for existing sessions after a failover, allowing sessions to continue with minimal or no interruption
It reduces the amount of data synchronized
It prevents any failover from occurring
questionPool.explanation: When you enable session synchronization, the new primary can resume communication for sessions after a failover event. The goal is for existing sessions to continue flowing through the new primary FortiGate with minimal or no interruption.

questionPool.question: Which task is exclusive to active-active mode for the primary FortiGate?
questionPool.explanation: In active-active mode only, a primary FortiGate is also responsible for distributing sessions to secondary members. This capability does not exist in active-passive mode.

questionPool.question: Can you make configuration changes on a secondary device in a synchronized cluster?
choices: No, only the primary accepts configuration changes

title: Failover types
content:
## Overview

FortiGate HA provides multiple types of failover protection to ensure that a secondary device can take over when the primary experiences a problem. Understanding the different failover types helps you design a resilient HA deployment and configure the right monitoring options for your environment.

![Failover types](diagram:0)

## Common Failover Types

**Device failover** occurs when the secondary devices stop receiving hello packets from the primary FortiGate. This indicates the primary is no longer reachable.

**Link failover** occurs when the link status of a monitored interface on the primary FortiGate goes down. You can configure the HA cluster to monitor one or more interfaces. If a monitored interface on the primary is unplugged or its link status goes down, a new primary FortiGate is elected.

**Remote link failover** uses the link health monitor feature to monitor the health of one or more interfaces against one or more servers that act as beacons. The primary FortiGate fails over if the accumulated penalty of all failed interfaces reaches the configured threshold.

**Memory-based failover**: triggered when memory utilization on the primary FortiGate reaches the configured threshold for the configured monitoring period.

**SSD failover**: triggers a failover if FortiOS detects Ext-fs errors on an SSD on the primary FortiGate.

## Failover Trigger Events

Multiple events can trigger an HA failover:

- Hardware or software failure on the primary FortiGate
- An issue on one of the interfaces on the primary
- An administrator-triggered failover

When a failover occurs, an event log is generated. Optionally, you can configure the device to also generate SNMP traps and alert emails.

## Session Pickup

Enabling session pickup allows active sessions to be seamlessly picked up by the new primary in the event of an HA failover. Users' sessions continue uninterrupted, and they will not notice that a failover occurred.

Note that there are limitations: sessions that terminate at the FortiGate itself — such as SSL VPN sessions and proxy sessions — cannot be handed off to another FortiGate and must be restarted on the new primary.

## Virtual MAC Addresses

To forward traffic correctly after a failover, a FortiGate HA solution uses virtual MAC addresses. When a primary joins an HA cluster, each interface is assigned a virtual MAC address based on the HA group ID, virtual cluster ID (if enabled), and interface index number.

Key behaviors:

- If two or more HA clusters are in the same broadcast domain with the same HA group ID, MAC address conflicts may occur — assign different HA group IDs to each cluster
- Upon failover, the new primary adopts the same virtual MAC addresses for the equivalent interfaces
- The new primary broadcasts gratuitous ARP packets, notifying the network that each virtual MAC address is now reachable through a different switch port
- The reserved HA management interface keeps its original MAC address and is NOT assigned a virtual MAC address

> **Key terms:** A configuration backup completion can trigger a failover test in some HA test scenarios.

title: Monitoring FortiGate HA
content:
## Overview

FortiGate provides both GUI and CLI tools to monitor the health and status of an HA cluster. Regular monitoring ensures you can detect synchronization issues, verify member roles, and access individual cluster members for administration. Understanding how to access secondary members and manage HA management interfaces is essential for day-to-day HA operations.

![Monitoring FortiGate HA](diagram:0)

## GUI Monitoring

The **HA page** in the FortiGate GUI shows important information about the health of your HA cluster. For each cluster member, it displays:

- Synchronization status
- Status, host name, serial number, and role
- Priority, uptime, and active sessions

From the HA page you can also remove a device from the cluster (which sets the device to standalone mode). You can enable additional columns to display checksum, CPU, and memory information.

You can also add the **HA Status widget** on the Dashboard page for a summary of the HA status on the device.

## CLI Monitoring: get system ha status

The `get system ha status` command displays comprehensive HA status information and is usually the first step when troubleshooting HA. The output includes:

- Cluster status, member model, HA mode in use, and cluster uptime
- Latest primary election events, results, and reasons
- Configuration sync status for each member
- System usage statistics: number of sessions each member handles, average CPU and memory usage
- Status information for heartbeat, monitored, and remote link interfaces
- Role, host name, serial number, and ID for each member

## CLI Monitoring: Checksum Commands

The `diagnose sys ha checksum` command tree lets you verify configuration sync status:

- `diagnose sys ha checksum cluster` — polls and displays the checksum of each member using the heartbeat interface (recommended for normal use)
- `diagnose sys ha checksum show` — shows the checksum of the local member (useful if heartbeat communication issues prevent the cluster command from showing all members)
- `diagnose sys ha checksum recalculate` — recalculates HA checksums when configurations appear in sync but checksums differ

FortiGate computes hash values for three configuration scopes: **global** (global settings, FortiGuard settings), **root** (settings specific to the root VDOM), and **all** (global plus all VDOMs). If all members show the exact same hash values for each scope, the configuration is in sync.

## Accessing Secondary Members

When cluster members share virtual IP addresses, connecting to any virtual IP always connects to the primary. Secondary members are not directly reachable over the network for SSH, HTTPS, or SNMP because all interfaces share the same IP addresses as the primary.

To access a secondary member's CLI, use `execute ha manage <member-id> <admin-username>` from the primary CLI. This tunnels into the secondary's CLI through the primary. Type `exit` to return to the primary's CLI prompt.

## HA Management Interfaces

FortiGate provides two options for direct member access regardless of HA role:

**Reserved HA management interface** (out-of-band): configure up to four dedicated management interfaces, each assigned a unique address per member. The reserved management interface routing is placed in a separate routing table, ensuring segmentation between data and management traffic. You can also use it for outbound management services such as SNMP traps, logs, and authentication requests.

**In-band HA management**: assign a unique management address to any user-traffic interface on a member without dedicating a separate interface. Configuration applied on a member is not synchronized to other cluster members for both options.

title: Overall diagnosis
content:
## Overview

Diagnosis is the process of finding the underlying cause of a problem. Before you can define any problem, you must first know what your network's normal behavior is. Normal is measured and defined in many ways: expected CPU and memory utilization, bandwidth, traffic volumes, network topology, traffic flow directions, which protocols are blocked or proxied, and the distribution of protocols and applications used during specific times of the day, week, or year.

When current behavior leaves the normal range, an abnormal event is happening. Establishing a baseline is therefore the first step in any diagnostic process.

![Overall diagnosis](diagram:0)

## Defining Normal: Network Diagrams and Baselines

The first step in defining what is normal for your network is creating and maintaining a network diagram. If you create a ticket with Fortinet Technical Support, a network diagram should be the first thing you attach. Network diagrams come in two types:

- **Physical diagram**: Shows how cables, ports, and devices are connected between buildings and cabinets
- **Logical diagram**: Shows relationships (usually at OSI layer 3) between virtual LANs, IP subnets, and routers; can also show application protocols such as HTTP or DHCP

When you configure devices and add them to the Security Fabric, these physical and logical topologies are available in the Security Fabric section of the FortiGate device.

Collecting ongoing performance data is equally important. For example, if traffic processing is suddenly slow and FortiGate CPU use is 75%, you need to know whether that is normal. If normal is 12–15%, there may be a problem. FortiGate provides tools such as FortiView monitors and dashboard widgets to monitor interface bandwidth and adjust the time frame to one hour, one day, or one week.

## CLI Commands for Current Status

CLI commands are valuable because you can use them through a local console even if network issues make GUI access slow or impossible. Key commands include:

- **`get system status`**: Provides general-purpose information including model, serial number, firmware version, host name, FortiGuard license status, system time, and versions of the FortiGuard antivirus, IPS, and IP reputation databases
- **`execute ping`** and **`execute traceroute`**: Used to test connectivity from FortiGate (for example, to FortiAnalyzer or FortiGuard)
- **`execute ping6`** / **`execute traceroute6`**: IPv6 equivalents

## Connectivity Testing Best Practices

Location matters when running tests — tests are accurate only if you use the same path as the traffic you are troubleshooting. To test the path *through* FortiGate, also use ping and tracert from the endpoint (Windows, Linux, or Mac OS X), not only from the FortiGate CLI.

If FortiGate can contact some hosts through port1 but not others, the problem is likely at the network layer rather than the physical or link layer. Because of NAT and routing, you might need to specify a different ping source IP address — the default address is the IP of the outgoing interface. If there is no response, verify that the target is configured to reply to ICMP echo requests.

> **Key terms:** The normal baseline includes typical CPU, memory, session count, and bandwidth — not the number of active administrator accounts.

> **Key terms:** To diagnose CPU at 75%, compare it against the normal baseline for that same time period.

> **Key terms:** Testing from the endpoint ensures you are using the same path as the traffic being troubleshot.

> **Key terms:** FortiGate built-in monitoring tools include FortiView monitors and dashboard widgets to track interface bandwidth.

title: The packet sniffer and debug flow
content:
## Overview

FortiGate includes the sniffer command, which is a useful tool when troubleshooting requires you to dig further to diagnose the source of the issue. The sniffer command can sniff packets on physical or virtual interfaces. If the sniffer command is set to `any`, it can sniff all available interfaces simultaneously.

You can use a filter to customize and narrow down the packets that you want to capture. The sniffer filter uses Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax.

![The packet sniffer and debug flow](diagram:0)

## The Packet Sniffer

The verbose setting has six verbosity levels:

- **1**: Print header of packets
- **2**: Print header and data from the IP header of the packets
- **3**: Print header and data from the Ethernet header of the packets
- **4**: Print header of packets with interface name
- **5**: Print header and data from IP of packets with interface name
- **6**: Print header and data from Ethernet of packets with interface name

To sniffer traffic on all interfaces, use the keyword `any` as the interface name. Stop the sniffer by pressing **Ctrl+C** and check for dropped packets. If there were dropped packets during the sniffer, not all traffic that matched the sniffer filter could be captured, so you might need to capture the traffic again using a stricter filter.

If you do not specify an option for the timestamp, the debug shows the time in seconds since it started running. You can prepend the local system time to easily correlate a packet with another recorded event.

The **Packet Capture** tool in the GUI allows you to view packet capture output in real time until you stop the capture process. After you stop the packet capture, you can export the output as a **pcap file**.

## Debug Flow

If FortiGate is dropping packets, a packet capture (sniffer) alone cannot identify the reason. To find the cause, you should use the **debug (packet) flow**. The debug flow shows, step-by-step, how the CPU is handling each packet.

To use the debug flow, follow these steps:

1. Define a filter
2. Enable debug output
3. Start the trace
4. Stop the trace when it is finished

A debug flow output for a TCP three-way handshake SYN packet shows:

- The packet arriving at FortiGate, indicating source and destination IP addresses, port numbers, and incoming interface
- FortiGate creating a session, indicating the session ID
- The route to the destination, indicating the next-hop IP address and outgoing interface
- The ID of the policy that matches and allows this traffic
- How source NAT is applied

For the SYN/ACK packet, the debug flow shows the ID of the existing session (matching the session created during the SYN packet) and how destination NAT is applied. If the packet is dropped by FortiGate, this debug shows the reason for that action.

## Hardware Offloading: NP and CP

FortiGate first performs security inspections such as ACL, HPE, and IP integrity header checking, handled by the **network processor (NP)** to minimize impact on the FortiGate CPU. The NP enhances performance by allowing offloaded sessions to bypass the CPU after the session is established and the session key is installed in the NP. The NP can also handle IPsec VPN encryption and decryption.

The **content processor (CP)** offloads tasks such as pattern matching for flow-based UTM inspection with the IPS engine, SSL/TLS decryption and encryption for deep SSL inspection, and IPsec encryption and decryption. For virtual FortiGate devices, the CPU handles all processes instead of offloading to NPs and CPs.

> **Key terms:** The Debug Flow GUI tool allows filtering completed output by time, message, or function.

title: CPU and memory usage
content:
## Overview

Not all network problems are connectivity failures. Sometimes, resource constraints within FortiGate devices are the root cause of latency and degraded performance. After eliminating physical media and bandwidth issues, you should check FortiGate resource usage — specifically CPU and memory. If usage is high, diagnostic tools can identify which feature or process is consuming the most resources.

![CPU and memory usage](diagram:0)

## Monitoring Processes

FortiGate provides several tools to inspect running processes and their resource consumption:

- The **process monitor** in the GUI lets you view, filter, sort, and terminate processes.
- The CLI command `diagnose sys top` lists processes consuming the most CPU or memory.
- Common processes include `ipsengine` and `scanunitd` (inspection), `fgfmd` (FortiGuard/FortiManager connections), `forticron` (scheduling), and management processes such as `newcli`, `miglogd`, `cmdb`, `sshd`, and `httpsd`.
- Press **Shift+P** to sort by highest CPU usage, and **Shift+M** to sort by highest RAM usage.

## Memory Conserve Mode

If memory usage becomes too high, FortiGate enters **memory conserve mode** to prevent the system from becoming unstable and inaccessible. Three configurable thresholds define this behavior:

- **Red threshold**: memory usage above this value triggers conserve mode.
- **Extreme threshold**: if memory usage exceeds this highest threshold, all new sessions are dropped.
- **Green threshold**: memory usage must fall below this value for FortiGate to exit conserve mode.

While in conserve mode, FortiGate takes protective actions:

- FortiGate does not accept configuration changes, because they might increase memory usage.
- FortiGate does not run any quarantine action, including forwarding suspicious files to FortiSandbox.
- The `av-failopen` setting controls antivirus proxy behavior: `off` blocks new sessions, `pass` (default) allows sessions without inspection, and `one-shot` bypasses AV even after leaving conserve mode — requiring a manual reset or restart.

## IPS Fail-Open Behavior

The `fail-open` setting under `config ips global` controls how the IPS engine behaves when its socket buffer is full — both in conserve mode and during any other IPS failure:

- **Enabled**: packets are transmitted but not inspected by IPS (bypass without inspection).
- **Disabled**: packets are dropped for new, incoming sessions.

The IPS engine handles all flow-based inspections, including application control. Note that **NTurbo does not support the fail-open setting** — if fail-open is triggered, sessions that would normally be accelerated with NTurbo are dropped even when fail-open is enabled.

To check whether FortiGate is currently in memory conserve mode, use the command `diagnose hardware sysinfo conserve`.
